title: FAQ > I bought a plugin. Where is my license?
text:
It is in an email from licenses@fruitlessresearch.com, sent within a few minutes of checkout. Check spam and
promotions. If it is not there, use **Can't find your license email?** on the downloads page or any plugin
page: enter the address you bought with and the same licenses are sent again. (The chat can send it too.)

title: FAQ > How do I activate a license?
text:
Each plugin has its own license line. Open the plugin, click the **FR mark** on its panel, paste that plugin's
line into the field, and reload the session. The panel says "Accepted - reload the session to activate", and
the license takes effect when the session reloads.

Or use the files: the email also attaches one `.frlicense` file per plugin. Put them in
`~/Library/Fruitless Research/licenses/` on a Mac or `%APPDATA%\Fruitless Research\licenses\` on Windows
(create the folder if it is missing) and reload the session. Every license in the folder is active at once.

title: FAQ > The folder doesn't exist / I can't find it.
text:
Both folders are hidden by default, so type the path instead of browsing. On a Mac, in Finder choose
**Go > Go to Folder** (Cmd-Shift-G) and paste `~/Library/Fruitless Research/licenses/`. On Windows, paste
`%APPDATA%\Fruitless Research\licenses\` into the address bar of any Explorer window. If `licenses` is not
there, create it.

title: FAQ > I bought the bundle. Do I get one license or many?
text:
One per plugin, all in the same email, each labeled with the plugin it belongs to. Paste each line into its
own plugin, or drop all the `.frlicense` files into the licenses folder at once.

title: FAQ > The panel says "Not a license for this plugin".
text:
That line belongs to a different plugin. Each license is labeled in the email with the plugin it is for;
paste the one that matches the plugin you have open.

title: FAQ > The panel says "Could not read that - paste the whole line".
text:
Part of the line was lost in copying. Copy the whole license line from the email, start to end, with nothing
added, and paste it again. If it still fails, use the `.frlicense` file instead.

title: FAQ > I pasted my license but it still says unlicensed.
text:
A license takes effect when the session reloads. Close and reopen the session (or remove and re-add the
plugin). If it still shows "Demo ended - not licensed" after a reload, check that the line is for this plugin,
or put the `.frlicense` file in the licenses folder. If none of that works, write to us.

title: FAQ > How many computers can I use it on?
text:
All the computers you personally own or control. There is no activation limit, no account, no dongle and no
online check. Copy your `.frlicense` files to each machine's licenses folder.

title: FAQ > I got a new computer. How do I move my license?
text:
There is nothing to deactivate on the old one. Install the plugins on the new computer and paste your license
lines or copy your `.frlicense` files there. If you no longer have the email, use **Can't find your license
email?** and the same licenses come again.

title: FAQ > Does a license expire? Do I need to be online?
text:
No and no. A license is checked on your own machine, it does not expire, and no server has to be running for
your session to open.

title: FAQ > How does the demo work?
text:
Every plugin runs complete for 14 days, counted from the first time you open that plugin's window.
Installing, scanning or loading a session does not start the clock. Nothing is disabled during the demo.

title: FAQ > What happens when the demo ends?
text:
The plugin keeps loading and passing audio, with a brief silence every so often to mark that it is
unlicensed, and a bar on the panel says so. It never mutes a track outright and never in the first 30 seconds
of playback. Your sessions still open. Paste a license and reload, and it stops.

title: FAQ > Is Clew really free?
text:
Yes. Clew is free: use **Get Clew** on its page, check out at $0, and the license arrives by email like any
other. It never expires.

title: FAQ > Are updates free?
text:
Yes. Updates to a plugin you have licensed are free, permanently. Your existing license works with every
new version.

title: FAQ > Does the bundle include future plugins?
text:
No. The bundle is the catalog on the day you buy it. A plugin released later is a separate purchase. If you
already own some plugins, see "I already own some plugins" below.

title: FAQ > I already own some plugins. Can I get the rest at the bundle price?
text:
Yes. On the pricing page, under **Already own some of these?**, enter the email you bought with. You get a
link that prices the bundle with what you already own taken off, at the bundle's own discount. The exact
amount is shown at checkout.

title: FAQ > Why was tax added at checkout?
text:
Prices are shown before tax. Your local sales tax, VAT or GST is added at checkout and shown in full before
you pay. Our payment provider (Paddle) is the merchant of record and handles the tax; its name is what
appears on your card statement.

title: FAQ > Can I get a refund?
text:
Yes, within 14 days of purchase, in full, with no reason needed and nothing to uninstall. Write to us. The
refund goes back to your original payment method, normally within five to ten business days.

title: FAQ > Can I give or sell my license to someone else?
text:
No. A license is personal and non-transferable, so it cannot be shared, resold or given away. If your
situation is unusual (a studio changing hands, say), write to us.

title: FAQ > I changed my email address / bought with an old address.
text:
Use **Can't find your license email?** with the address you bought with; the licenses go to that inbox. If
you no longer have access to it, write to us from your new address with your order details and we will sort
it out by hand.

title: FAQ > Do you have education, multi-seat or studio pricing?
text: Not as a listed price. Write to us with what you need.

title: FAQ > Can I use it in commercial work?
text: Yes. Anything you make with the plugins is yours, with no royalty and no credit required.

title: Manual > Before you start > Installing
text:
{{COUNT_WORD_CAP}} plugins. Each does one thing. Each is voiced by ear against a specific
piece of hardware, or against measurement where there is no hardware to compare with,
rather than assembled from generic building blocks.

| | |
|:--|:--|
| **Trammel** | A fast solid-state compressor. Fixed threshold, driven from the input. |
| **Remanence** | Output-transformer coloration, in three voicings. |
| **Amnesia** | A bucket-brigade analog delay, with tap tempo and host sync. |
| **Fifty-Fifty** | A Japanese half-track stereo reel-to-reel tape machine. |
| **Jointer** | A clipper that clips the waveform your listener hears. |
| **Firmament** | A plate reverb, solved from the physics of the sheet rather than sampled. |
| **Keelson** | A bus compressor with switchable output iron. |
| **Clew** | A spring reverb, built from the physics of the coil rather than sampled. |
| **Undercroft** | A room reverb. You set the room's dimensions and surfaces, and it works out the rest. |

**Every plugin runs complete for 14 days from the first time you open it.**
Nothing is disabled in that window. See *The demo, and your license*. Click the
**FR mark** on any panel to see its version, build date and license status.

**macOS.** Run the `.pkg` installer and choose the formats you want. Or unzip the
drag-and-drop archive and copy the plugins yourself:

title: Manual > Before you start > Installing
text:
- `.component` files go in `~/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/Components` (Logic, GarageBand, MainStage)
- `.vst3` files go in `~/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/VST3` (Live, Cubase, Reaper, Studio One, Bitwig)
- `.aaxplugin` files go in `/Library/Application Support/Avid/Audio/Plug-Ins` (Pro Tools)

The files are named `<Plugin>_FR`: `Trammel_FR.component`, `Trammel_FR.vst3`. The
suffix keeps them from landing on another maker's plugin of the same name. Your DAW
shows `Trammel`; the suffix is only on the file. If you are upgrading from an
installation older than this manual, the installer removes the old-named files for
you. If you copied them in by hand, delete the old `<Plugin>.component`, `.vst3` and
`.aaxplugin` yourself, or your DAW will list each plugin twice.

Both installers can leave a plugin out. Tick *Choose individual plugins* and untick
what you do not want. Left alone, they install every plugin in each format you chose.
A plugin whose destination already holds another maker's bundle starts unticked, and
the installer says why.

Installing all three formats is fine. The builds are signed and notarized by Apple,
so there is no Gatekeeper warning and nothing to do in Terminal.

The AAX folder is the only one outside your home folder, so copying into it by hand
asks for an administrator password. The installer does that part for you.

**Windows.** Unzip and copy the `<Plugin>_FR.vst3` folders into
`C:\Program Files\Common Files\VST3`. Delete any older `<Plugin>.vst3` of ours first.
Pro Tools on Windows is not supported yet; see *Requirements*.

title: Manual > Before you start > Installing
text:
Then restart your DAW, and rescan plugins if it does not do that on its own.
Everything appears under the manufacturer name **Fruitless Research**.

Step-by-step instructions ship with the plugins as `INSTALL.txt`.

title: Manual > Before you start > Requirements
text:
- **macOS** 10.15 (Catalina) or later. One universal download runs natively on
  Apple Silicon and Intel Macs. Audio Unit, VST3 and AAX.
- **Windows** 10 or later, 64-bit, VST3 only.

Pro Tools is supported on macOS only. The Windows AAX build needs signing with
Windows tooling, which is not in place yet.

**The Windows build is newer and has had less time in front of people than the
macOS one.** The same automated tests build and check it, and they report the same
numbers on both platforms. But macOS is where these plugins have been used in real
sessions. If something looks wrong on Windows, especially window scaling or fonts,
please report it. See *Feedback*.

title: Manual > Before you start > The demo, and your license
text:
Every plugin runs **complete for 14 days**, counted from the first time you open
that plugin's window. Installing it, scanning it, or loading a session that
contains it does not start the clock. Nothing is disabled during the demo, and
nothing stops part-way through a session. The demo processes audio identically to the
licensed plugin.

When the 14 days are up, the plugin keeps loading and keeps passing audio, with a
brief silence every so often to mark that it is unlicensed. That is deliberate. A
plugin that quietly stopped processing would let you finish a mix and ship it
wrong. It never mutes a track outright, it never happens in the first 30 seconds of
playback, and a bar across the panel says what is happening.

**Each plugin has its own license.** A bundle purchase emails you one per plugin,
each labeled with the plugin it belongs to. Click the **FR mark** on a panel, paste
that plugin's line into the field, and reload the session. Activation takes effect
on reload, and the panel tells you so.

**Or use the files.** The same licenses are attached to that email as
`.frlicense` files, one per plugin. Put them in this folder (create it if it is
not there) and reload the session. Everything in the folder is active at once:

- macOS: `~/Library/Fruitless Research/licenses/`
- Windows: `%APPDATA%\Fruitless Research\licenses\`

title: Manual > Before you start > The demo, and your license
text:
Both folders are hidden by default, so type the path rather than hunting for it.
On a Mac, in Finder choose **Go > Go to Folder** (Cmd-Shift-G) and paste the path.
The `~` stands for your home folder, and Finder fills it in. On Windows, paste the
path into the address bar of any Explorer window. `%APPDATA%` stands for your own
`AppData\Roaming` folder, and Windows fills it in.

Both routes do the same thing. Pasting is quickest for one plugin on one machine.
The files are easier for a second machine or a whole studio. There is no
drag-onto-the-panel step; the plugin reads whatever is in the folder.

A license is checked on your own machine. There is no account, no activation
limit, no dongle, and no server that has to be running for your session to open.
It does not expire, and you can install it on every machine you work on.

title: Manual > Controls every plugin shares
text:
The {{COUNT_WORD}} plugins are built on shared code, so the frame around each panel
works the same way in all of them. Read this once here rather than {{COUNT_WORD}}
times later.

**GUI size: 75% / 100% / 125% / 150% / 200%.** Drag the grip in the bottom-right
corner **of the panel**, or right-click anywhere on the background for the list.
The window has no resize edge. The panel comes in those five sizes and the window
is always the size of the panel, so a free-form drag could only leave a
gap. Between the steps, the fine lines and indicator dots would fall on half pixels
and look soft, so nothing in between is offered.

**The size is shared by all {{COUNT_WORD}} plugins and remembered between sessions.**
Set it once and every plugin opens that way from then on. Windows already on
screen keep the size they were opened at. A size too large for your display is
grayed out rather than missing, so the list looks the same on every machine.

Nothing moves at any size. The panel is drawn larger or smaller, and every control
stays where you learned it.

title: Manual > Controls every plugin shares
text:
**Look.** Each plugin opens in a look of its own, named in the same right-click
menu under **LOOK**. Trammel's is *Van Nuys*, Undercroft's *Lastingham*. The other
entry, **Classic**, is the line's original dark panel, the same on every plugin.
Like the size, the choice is shared by all {{COUNT_WORD}} plugins and remembered.
Choose Classic in one and every plugin opens that way until you choose its own
look again. The window you chose it in changes at once. Windows already open
elsewhere change the next time you open them. The look is not saved in your
session, so a project opens the same on any machine.

A look changes nothing you hear and no setting. Every parameter, preset, reading
and automation lane is the same in both. Two panels draw one control differently.
In its own look, Firmament's **Decay** is the plate's damping wheel rather than a
knob, and Fifty-Fifty shows a turning tape reel where the output arc would be, with
the output level printed above it. In Classic both are the ordinary knob and arc.

**Knob scales.** Some looks number the scale around each knob. The numbers are
real values in the knob's own unit, at their true positions, not 0 to 10. Where a
look colors its knobs by job, a **red knob is always the output**.

title: Manual > Controls every plugin shares
text:
**Preset bar.** The wide strip under the title shows the current preset. Click it
for the menu: save, rename, delete, and the factory **Default**, which resets every
parameter. Some plugins add factory presets of their own below it (Jointer ships
the two delivery ceilings). Those cannot be overwritten or deleted, and loading one
resets everything else to its default first, so a factory preset means the same
thing however you left the plugin. The arrows on either side step through your
presets.

**Naming a preset `Group/Name` files it under a submenu.** Save something as
`TW Walsh/Warm Bus` and it appears under a **TW Walsh** entry in the menu rather
than in the flat list. It also lives in a matching folder on disk, so moving a file
between folders regroups it. Presets without a slash behave as before.

Presets are plain files on disk, so you can back them up or pass them to someone
else:

- macOS: `~/Library/Fruitless Research/<Plugin>/Presets`
- Windows: `%APPDATA%\Fruitless Research\<Plugin>\Presets`

**Oversampling: OFF / 2X / 4X / 8X.** The six plugins that distort do so on purpose.
Distortion makes harmonics above the sample rate, and those fold back down as
aliasing unless they are dealt with. Oversampling runs the nonlinear part of the
plugin at a higher internal rate, so the harmonics have somewhere to go.

title: Manual > Controls every plugin shares
text:
**4X is the default and is the right answer nearly always.** Go to 8X for a final
mix or master if the CPU is free. Drop to 2X or OFF when you are tracking and want
the latency down, or when you have many instances open. Higher settings cost CPU
and add latency, which your DAW compensates for automatically. It is not a tone
control. If 8X sounds different from 4X on your material, what you are hearing is
aliasing being removed.

**Firmament has no oversampling control.** A reverb built from resonators is
linear. It generates no new harmonics, so there is no aliasing to prevent, and
oversampling would only cost CPU. The one nonlinear thing in it, the **Drive**
stage, oversamples itself at four times the rate (twice at 88.2 and 96 kHz), on
one channel, for well under a percent of a core.

**Jointer is the other exception: 4X / 8X / 16X, defaulting to 8X, with no OFF.**
Its oversampling is not only anti-aliasing. It is how the plugin sees the peaks
between your samples in the first place. Switching it off would not make the
plugin cheaper; it would make it a different and less accurate plugin. So the
option does not exist.

**Bypass.** Latency-compensated and click-free, so A/B comparisons stay
time-aligned and level-honest. Your DAW's own bypass is wired to the same thing.

title: Manual > Controls every plugin shares
text:
**Auto Gain.** On every plugin except Jointer, a small lit dot labeled `AUTO GAIN`
sits above the knobs. Switch it on and the plugin matches its output loudness to
its input. Bypassing it then answers *is this better?* rather than *is this
louder?*, which is the only comparison worth making. The number beside it is the
gain being applied.

It works from **K-weighted loudness** (the LUFS measurement used for delivery),
not from gain reduction. A makeup derived from gain reduction compensates *peak*
reduction, which stops matching the moment the crest factor changes. And
saturation and delay have no gain reduction to derive from at all. Working from
loudness, the same control behaves the same on every plugin that has it.

Five things worth knowing:

title: Manual > Controls every plugin shares
text:
- **It adds no latency.** The measurement watches the signal go past. Nothing is
  delayed, and your bypass comparison stays time-aligned.
- **It takes a moment to settle.** The level is right within about half a second
  and settles over roughly three, because that is the window the loudness
  measurement runs over. Move a knob a long way and you will see it catch up.
- **It knows a tail from a silence.** This is the hard part, and it is why the
  control behaves on a delay and a reverb, not only on a compressor. When you stop
  playing, a compressor's output stops with you. A delay's repeats and a plate's
  tail keep going, so for a few seconds the plugin puts out loudness against an
  input of nothing. A loudness matcher that ignores that reads the gap as *far too
  loud*, pulls the trim down, ducks your own tail, and lets go again on the next
  note: a slow tremolo locked to your phrasing, worst on sparse parts with long
  repeats. On Amnesia and Firmament the measurement also watches a short window on
  the input, so it can tell *you stopped playing* from *there is no signal*, and
  holds its correction steady through the tail. Measured on 4-second phrases with
  5-second gaps, that is the difference between the trim moving up to **8.8 dB**
  during a gap and it moving **less than half a dB**.
- **It holds still.** Because it compares input against output, the correction is
  a ratio. It is set by where your knobs are, not by how busy the part is. A sparse
  verse and a dense chorus measure within a tenth of a dB of each other, and
  starting playback from five different points in a song lands on the same trim
  every time. Two bounces of the same session will match, though both share the
  same ramp at the start. That is what **Commit** below is for.
- **It takes the output knob out of play, and dims it to say so.** A level control
  in front of a stage that normalizes level is canceled by it. So while
  Auto Gain is on, the knob it cancels is faded and inactive. On Remanence,
  Fifty-Fifty, Amnesia, Firmament and Keelson that is **Output**, at any Mix
  setting, because their trim is applied after the wet/dry blend. On Trammel it is
  **Makeup**, and only at **Mix 100%**. Its makeup sits *before* the blend, so at
  lower Mix settings it is still a real wet/dry balance and stays live. Turn Auto
  Gain off to get the knob back.

title: Manual > Controls every plugin shares
text:
It is **off by default** and off in every preset, so nothing you have already
saved will recall differently.

**On Amnesia and Firmament, use it as an insert, not on a send.** It compares what
goes in against what comes out, so it works when the plugin sits on a track with
Mix below 100%. On a fully wet send there is no dry signal in the output to match
against, and the comparison stops meaning anything.

**Commit, and why you want it before you bounce.** Next to the readout is a
`COMMIT` button. Press it and the trim you can see is folded into the plugin's
output trim, and Auto Gain switches itself off. The level does not change. What
changes is that the same gain is now a fixed number on a knob, instead of
something worked out live.

That matters for one reason. **Auto Gain does not remember its trim between
sessions.** Every time you reopen a session, reload the plugin, or start an
offline bounce, it begins from nothing. For roughly the first second it applies no
correction, then catches up. Measured on a plugin that had settled at +6 dB, the
first moments of a render come out a full 6 dB off, and are within half a dB after
about 0.9 seconds.

If your material starts with silence or a count-in, that second is absorbed and
you will never see it. If it starts on the downbeat, that second is in the file. A
committed trim is a fixed gain from the first sample, so there is nothing to catch
up on.

Three things it refuses to do, and it says which:

title: Manual > Controls every plugin shares
text:
- **Before it has settled.** For the first few seconds the button is faded. The
  trim is still a rough estimate, and committing it would replace a wrong level
  you can see ramping with a wrong level you cannot see at all. Let it settle,
  then commit.
- **On Trammel below Mix 100%.** Its Makeup is applied to the compressed signal
  before the parallel blend, so folding the number in would change the wet/dry
  balance rather than the output level. At Mix 100% it commits normally. The other
  plugins apply their trim after the blend and commit at any Mix.
- **Past the end of the knob.** Output stops at 24 dB. If the trim does not fit,
  it commits as much as it can and says `AT LIMIT` rather than letting you believe
  the level matched. Check the Output knob to see where it landed.

It is an ordinary parameter move, so it lands in undo and in automation as if
you had turned the knob.

**Jointer does not have it**, deliberately. A stage that turns the output up would
break the ceiling, which is the one thing that plugin guarantees.

**Mix.** Where a plugin has one, it blends the processed signal against the clean
input. The blend happens *inside* the oversampled section, so the two paths stay
sample-aligned. There is no phase smear at intermediate settings. Parallel
processing does what you expect.

title: Manual > Controls every plugin shares
text:
**Output meter.** On Trammel, Remanence, Amnesia, Clew and Fifty-Fifty, the arc on
the right is the plugin's output level. The marks at the top of the scale are the
last few dB before clipping. The others show a measurement there instead:
Jointer's clip trace and damage report, Firmament's decay curve, Keelson's gain
reduction, and Undercroft's room. In its own look, Fifty-Fifty's arc becomes a
tape reel that turns while the transport runs, with the output level printed in
its header.

title: Manual > Where each plugin goes
text:
If you have never had a mix chain explained to you, this chapter is the map. Each
plugin's own chapter has a **Starting points** section with settings. This one says
which plugin to reach for, in what order, and how to tell whether it is helping.
It assumes nothing except that you can hear.

title: Manual > Where each plugin goes > The order
text:
A mix is built in layers, and the plugins sort into three jobs:

| Job | Where | Plugins |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Shaping a single track | on the track | Trammel, Remanence, Amnesia, Firmament, Clew, Undercroft |
| Holding the mix together | on the mix bus | Keelson, Fifty-Fifty, Remanence |
| Making it loud, safely | last, on the master | Jointer |

Work in that order. Fix tracks before you glue the mix. Glue the mix before you
make it loud. Every plugin has a **Mix** knob and a meter, and the way to use any
of them is the same: set it, then **bypass it and listen**. If bypassing changes
nothing you can name, turn it down or take it off. Doing less is not a failure.
It is usually the right answer.

title: Manual > Where each plugin goes > On a track
text:
**A vocal or a lead synth that will not sit still.** Trammel, the *Vocals*
starting point. Look for 4 to 6 dB on the meter on the loud phrases and nothing on
the quiet ones. Then raise Makeup until bypassing it sounds the same level, only
steadier.

**Drums that sound like a drum machine when you wanted a band.** Trammel on the
drum bus, *Drum bus, glued*, Mix 60 to 70%. Or Remanence *Punch* for the snap
without the pumping.

**A synth bass that is all note and no weight.** Remanence, *Weight*. Then stop.
Low end stacks up faster than anything else in a mix, and the next plugin's job is
to take some back out.

**A dry vocal that sounds pasted on.** Amnesia's *Slapback* is the oldest trick in
records and still the best one. If it wants space rather than an echo, use
Firmament's *Vocal plate* with the pre-delay left in. The pre-delay keeps the
words in front.

**A pad that needs to move.** Amnesia's *Chorus, not delay*. Anything with
sustained tones and nothing much happening.

**A guitar or a snare that wants a room it never had.** Clew's *Amp Tank* on the
track, Mix around 25%. Where Firmament is a space, Clew is a sound. The drip and
the splash are meant to be heard, so if it disappears into the mix, turn it up
rather than reaching for the plate.

**A close-miked take that needs to be in a room, not on a reverb.** Undercroft's
*Small room* or *Live room* on the track, Mix 15 to 25%. Firmament and Clew are
objects with a sound of their own. Undercroft is the room the take was never
recorded in. Set the size of the space you wish you had and leave the decay to the
walls.

title: Manual > Where each plugin goes > On the mix bus
text:
**The whole thing feels like separate tracks.** Keelson at its factory default
(2:1, AUTO release). This is the setting it was built for. You want 2 to 3 dB on
the loudest sections and the meter resting near zero between them.

**It is clean but it is not a record yet.** Fifty-Fifty, *Mix bus glue*. What it
does is small: a little softening on transients, a little thickness at the bottom.
That is the difference between a session and a mix. Level-match with Output, then
bypass it and listen. If you cannot hear it, try *Just the softening* and trust it.

**Do not stack both to "warm it up".** One of them, at a setting you can hear,
beats both at settings you cannot. Fifty-Fifty on several *tracks* at low settings
is a different sound from one instance on the bus, and worth trying on a synthpop
mix where everything is already clean.

title: Manual > Where each plugin goes > On the master
text:
**Jointer goes last, at the sample rate you are delivering.** Load *Streaming
(-1.0 dBTP)* and bring Drive up while watching two numbers. `LOUDNESS ADDED` is
what you are buying and `DISTORTION ADDED` is what it costs. When the second
climbs faster than the first, you have found the price of loud on this mix.

"Radio ready" is mostly this step plus not having done too much before it. A mix
that already fits together needs little here. A mix that does not cannot be fixed
here. If you are pushing Drive to make the mix sound finished, the problem is
upstream.

title: Manual > Where each plugin goes > Reading the numbers
text:
Every meter in these plugins is measured from the audio, not estimated, so you
can use them to check yourself rather than to be reassured. Three are worth
watching until they mean something to you:

- **Gain reduction** (the compressors): how much is being turned down, right now.
  Too much all the time means the threshold is wrong. Too much on one element only
  means that element is too loud in the mix, which is a fader problem, not a
  compressor problem.
- **Distortion added** (Jointer, Remanence, Fifty-Fifty): how far the output
  differs from the input, as a number. It is not a judgment; a fair amount of it
  is what "warm" means. But it stops climbing quietly.
- **The output level** (the arc, or the figure in the header): if it reads above 0
  before Jointer, something upstream is too hot. Turn that down. Do not fix it at
  the end.

title: Manual > Trammel
text: A fast solid-state compressor. Fixed threshold, driven from the input.

title: Manual > Trammel > Controls
text:
| Control | Range | Default | What it does |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Input** | -12 to +36 dB | +12 | Drives the signal into the fixed threshold. This is the amount-of-compression control. |
| **SC HPF** | 20 to 185 Hz | 20 = off | A highpass on the detector only; the audio is untouched. Stops kick and bass from ducking the whole mix. |
| **Attack** | 0.02 to 0.8 ms | 0.100 | Time to clamp. The bottom of the range is instant; the top lets transients through. |
| **Slow** | off · on | off | A fixed 12 ms attack, beyond the knob's range, so transients get through whole. While it is lit, **Attack** is out of the circuit and dimmed. See *Notes*. |
| **Release** | 50 to 1100 ms | 250 | Time to let go. Short settings breathe and pump on purpose. |
| **Ratio** | 2:1 · 4:1 · 8:1 · 12:1 · 20:1 · All | 4:1 | How hard it holds. **All** is the all-buttons-in mode: a ratio between 12:1 and 20:1 with a distorted, aggressive knee. |
| **Makeup** | -24 to +24 dB | 0.0 | Gain on the compressed path, applied before the Mix blend, so it does nothing at Mix 0. |
| **Mix** | 0 to 100% | 100 | Parallel compression. 100% is fully compressed. |
| **Auto Gain** | off · on | off | Matches output loudness to input, so an A/B compares tone rather than level. Dims **Makeup** at Mix 100% while on. See *Controls every plugin shares*. |
| **Key** | input · sidechain | input | No control. Route a signal into the plugin's sidechain input in your host and the compressor follows it instead of its own input. See *Notes*. |

title: Manual > Trammel > Controls
text:
The detector is stereo-linked. Both channels take the same gain reduction, so the
stereo image does not wander. The signal path adds 2nd- and 3rd-harmonic
saturation. It is subtle at low Input and becomes part of the sound as you drive
it.

title: Manual > Trammel > Readings
text:
GAIN REDUCTION
:   A scrolling trace, not a needle. It shows the last few seconds, not only the
    current value, so you can see the shape of what the compressor is doing:
    grabbing transients and letting go, or sitting on the track. Watch it while
    you change Attack and Release. It is the fastest way to learn what those two
    knobs do.

KEY INT
:   The detector is following the plugin's own input.

KEY EXT
:   A lit dot and `KEY EXT`: the detector is following a sidechain. The key's
    level is drawn faintly behind the trace, so you can see what the compressor
    is reacting to.

OUTPUT
:   The arc on the right is the plugin's output level. The marks at the top of
    the scale are the last few dB before clipping.

title: Manual > Trammel > Starting points
text:
**Vocals, in front of the mix.** Ratio 4:1, Attack around 0.3 ms, Release 250
ms. Bring Input up until the trace shows 4 to 6 dB on the loud phrases, then
match level with Makeup.

**Drum bus, glued.** Ratio 4:1, Attack at its slowest, Release 100 to 150 ms, SC
HPF around 80 Hz so the kick stops driving the detector. Mix 60 to 70% keeps the
transients intact.

**Room mics, obliterated.** Ratio All, Input high, Attack fastest, Release fast.
This is the classic destructive setting. Use it at 100% Mix on something you are
blending in underneath a clean kit.

**Bass or a bus, ridden not squashed.** Ratio 2:1, Slow on, Release around 400
ms. Every transient arrives whole and the level underneath is held. If you can
hear it working, the Input is too high.

title: Manual > Trammel > Notes > The idea
text:
FET compressors earned their reputation on speed. An optical compressor eases into
gain reduction. A field-effect transistor (FET) clamps down in tens of
microseconds: fast enough to catch the leading edge of a snare, and fast enough
that the compression becomes part of the sound rather than a correction applied to
it. Push one hard and it does not politely limit. It thickens, distorts a little,
and pulls the whole track forward.

Those units also refused to give you a threshold knob. **There is no threshold
here either.** The threshold is fixed, and Input drives the signal into it.
Turning Input up gives more compression, and Makeup gives the level back. That
sounds like a missing feature. It is the reason the plugin is fast to use: one
knob for how much, one knob for how loud.

That is where the name comes from. A trammel is a thing that restrains; the word
survives mostly in its negative, *untrammeled*, meaning unrestricted. It is also a
real object: the adjustable pot-hook over a hearth, which sets a fixed height and
holds it. You move the pot to the hook rather than the hook to the pot. The
threshold here works the same way. It does not come to you; you drive the signal
up to it.

title: Manual > Trammel > Notes > The sidechain
text:
Route a signal into the plugin's sidechain input in your host (Pro Tools' key
input, Logic's side chain menu, Live's Audio From). The compressor follows that
signal instead of its own input from the first moment it carries signal. The
display's header reads `KEY EXT` and draws the key's level behind the gain
reduction. With nothing routed, nothing changes. Input still sets how hard the key
hits the threshold, and SC HPF filters the key as it would the input.

Once a key has carried signal, the compressor stays on it until playback restarts
or you bypass and un-bypass the plugin. If you remove the source mid-session, the
header still reads `KEY EXT` and the compression stops. It does not go back to
the input on its own.

title: Manual > Trammel > Notes > The slow attack, and the 2:1
text:
Some later revisions of the classic hardware ship the slow attack as a switch at
10 ms. Studios that modify their own units put it at the Attack knob's off
detent, and 12 ms is one such studio's figure. While Slow is lit, the Attack
readout says 12.0 ms. The 2:1 ratio is also a later addition, for leveling that
is not meant to be heard.

title: Manual > Remanence
text: Output-transformer coloration, in three voicings.

title: Manual > Remanence > Controls
text:
| Control | Range | Default | What it does |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Drive** | -12 to +24 dB | 0.0 | How hard you hit the core. Near-clean at 0; the coloration blooms as you push. |
| **Flavor** | Punch · Weight · Clean | Punch | Which transformer voicing. See *Notes*. |
| **Mix** | 0 to 100% | 100 | Parallel coloration. |
| **Output** | -24 to +24 dB | 0.0 | Final trim, applied after the mix, so it works at any Mix setting unless Auto Gain is on. |
| **Auto Gain** | off · on | off | Matches output loudness to input, so an A/B compares tone rather than level. No latency; settles over about 3 s. Dims **Output** while on. See *Controls every plugin shares*. |

The voicing is gentle at nominal level on purpose. This is a transformer, not a
distortion box. At Drive 0 it is a subtle thing you notice most when you bypass
it. The range lives in the top half of the Drive knob.

title: Manual > Remanence > Readings
text:
HARMONIC SIGNATURE
:   The harmonic series the plugin is generating right now: the 2nd through 5th
    harmonics, with `ODD` and `EVEN` orders colored differently. They are
    measured against a 100 Hz probe tone and read in dB relative to the
    fundamental. The display tracks live input and rests when there is silence,
    so it sits flat until you play something through it.

    The fundamental itself is not drawn. It is the reference everything else is
    measured against, so its bar would always be full height and would spend a
    fifth of the plot restating the axis. The probe is at 100 Hz rather than the
    usual 1 kHz because this plugin's mechanism is low-frequency pre-emphasis.
    A 1 kHz measurement would be accurate about a frequency where the effect
    barely operates. At Punch with Drive at 0, the 3rd harmonic reads -32.9 dB
    at 100 Hz against -47.5 dB at 1 kHz. That difference is the whole point.

    This is the fastest way to hear and see what a flavor is doing. Feed it a
    sustained low note and turn Drive up. Even-order content leads at low
    drive, and odd order takes over as the core saturates. That transition is
    the character of a transformer, and on most plugins you have to guess at
    it.

OUTPUT
:   The arc on the right is the plugin's output level. The marks at the top of
    the scale are the last few dB before clipping.

title: Manual > Remanence > Starting points
text:
**Mix bus warmth.** Clean, Drive 0 to +3, Mix 100%. Level-match with Output, then
bypass and listen. If you cannot hear a difference when bypassing, that is the
correct amount for a master.

**Bass and kick weight.** Weight, Drive +6 to +12. The LF-first saturation does
the work here.

**Snare and room attack.** Punch, Drive +9 or more, Mix around 70% to keep the
transient.

title: Manual > Remanence > Notes > The idea
text:
Every classic console has iron in it. The signal leaves each stage through an
output transformer, and that transformer is not transparent. Its core saturates
at low frequencies before it does anywhere else. It adds harmonics that shift in
character as you drive it. It resonates somewhere above the audible band, and it
loses a little at both ends. None of this was a design goal. It is what
transformers do, and it is a large part of why old consoles sound like old
consoles.

This plugin is that stage on its own, with nothing else attached: no
compressor, no EQ, no channel strip. **Flavor** picks which piece of iron you
are running through.

The important design decision: the flavors are the same engine with different
parameters, not three separate algorithms. So they sit on a continuous scale
with each other. The spread between them carries the range, from punchy to
thick to fat, rather than each one being an isolated preset.

**Remanence** is the magnetism left behind in an iron core after the signal that
put it there has gone. That lag is the core's memory of where it has just been.
It is why a transformer is not a fixed curve you could draw once and apply. It
responds to what came immediately before, which is what makes iron sound like a
thing being pushed rather than a filter being applied. Modeling that memory,
rather than a static shape, is the whole engine.

title: Manual > Remanence > Notes > Flavors
text:
**Punch.** The punchiest and the fastest. Grit appears at low levels. Low
harmonics dominate when clean and shift to odd order as you push, and the top
end runs almost all the way out. Use it when you want attack and presence.

**Weight.** The strongest coloration of the three, and the one that behaves most
like big iron. The low end saturates first and hardest. The top is rolled and
silky rather than open. Use it when you want weight and a sense of the signal
having been through something.

**Clean.** Clean until you drive it, then fat. Huge bandwidth, the least low-mid
harmonic content, and only a slight smoothing at the top. Use it when you want
the character without giving up clarity. It is the mastering-friendly one.

title: Manual > Amnesia
text: A bucket-brigade analog delay, with tap tempo and host sync.

title: Manual > Amnesia > Controls
text:
| Control | Range | Default | What it does |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Delay** | 30 to 1500 ms | 350 | The delay time in Manual. Moving it slews the pitch of the repeats. In Tap and Sync this knob becomes **Nudge**. |
| **Nudge** | -33.3 to +33.3% | 0 | Pushes or pulls the repeats around the tapped or synced grid. Double-click lands on the grid. Only active in Tap and Sync. See *Notes*. |
| **Tempo** | Manual · Tap · Sync | Manual | Who sets the time: the knob, your taps, or the host. See *Notes*. |
| **Tap Divide** | 1/4. · 1/4 · 1/8. · 1/8 · 1/16 | 1/4 | The note value a tapped or synced tempo resolves to. Inactive in Manual mode. |
| **Triplet** | off · on | off | Swaps the two dotted cells for triplets (1/4. becomes 1/4T, 1/8. becomes 1/8T). Straight notes are unaffected. |
| **Feedback** | 0 to 100% | 59 | How many repeats. The knob is an audio taper: the top quarter is the self-oscillation zone, and it limits softly rather than screaming. See *Notes*. |
| **Modulation** | Off · Chorus · Vibrato | Off | Chorus modulates around the delay. Vibrato is the pitch-moving version. |
| **Mod Rate** | 0.05 to 10 Hz | 1.00 | Speed of the modulation LFO. Chorus lives around 0.5 to 2 Hz, vibrato around 4 to 7 Hz. Dimmed while Modulation is Off. |
| **Mod Depth** | 0 to 100% | 0 | Depth of the modulation, calibrated by measurement. Depth and rate multiply; pushing both is the siren, on purpose. Dimmed while Modulation is Off. See *Notes*. |
| **Tap 2** | Mono · 1/4. · 1/4 · 1/8. · 1/8 · 1/16 | Mono | The stereo image, on one stepped knob. Mono is the same echo on both sides. Any note value is a second tap on the right at that value. See *Notes*. |
| **Mix** | 0 to 100% | 40 | Delay against dry. |
| **Output** | -24 to +24 dB | 0.0 | Final trim. |
| **Auto Gain** | off · on | off | Matches output loudness to input, so an A/B compares tone rather than level. No latency; settles over about 3 s. Dims **Output** while on. See *Controls every plugin shares*. |

title: Manual > Amnesia > Readings
text:
The display has two faces. Click it to switch. The plugin remembers which you
chose.

BUCKET BRIGADE - LIVE
:   The delay line itself: the two delay chips in series that the hardware
    used, lit from behind, with the charge in flight drawn on the chips. What
    you played marches across the first chip, over the trace, across the second
    and out. Then it comes back into the first chip, fainter, through the
    feedback. With Tap 2 at a note value, a marker on the chips shows where it
    picks the right channel off the line.

CLOCK
:   Printed top right of the live face: the clock the delay implies. Moving
    Delay or turning Modulation up makes the charge speed up and slow down as
    the clock does.

REPEATS
:   The echo train the plugin will produce: the dry hit plus six repeats,
    spaced by the resolved delay time, which is printed top right. Each repeat
    is drawn at its measured level in dB relative to what went in. The scale
    runs from -60 dB to a little above unity. The 0 dB line means as loud as
    what you played, and a bar above it means the delay is regenerating. With
    Tap 2 at a note value, the right side's train is drawn too, as hollow bars
    starting at its own time, and the header prints both times, L and R.

TONE
:   The figure at the bottom right of the Repeats face. The bars are colored by
    their measured tone, from bright cooling to a dark ember, and this figure
    states it. A 350 ms setting reads `TONE 1.4k -> 563`.

title: Manual > Amnesia > Readings
text:
OUTPUT
:   The arc on the right is the plugin's output level. The marks at the top of
    the scale are the last few dB before clipping.

Two things the Repeats face shows that are easy to get wrong by ear:

- **Feedback does not change how loud the first repeat is.** It sets how many
  you get. The first echo comes back at the same level whether Feedback is at
  0% or 100%. At 0% you get one repeat, and it is not quiet.
- **Delay time is a tone control.** The bucket-brigade's filter tracks its
  clock. So a long delay is a dark delay before any repeat has decayed, and
  every repeat darkens again on the way round.

The face is most useful in Sync and Tap modes. It tells you what the
subdivision resolved to before you have to hear it to find out.

title: Manual > Amnesia > Starting points
text:
**Slapback.** Load the **Slapback** preset (Manual, 110 ms, one repeat) and set
Mix around 30%. Anywhere in 90 to 120 ms works. The preset leaves Mix to you
because the right amount depends on the source.

**Dub throw.** Sync, 1/4 or dotted-1/8, Feedback 80 to 85%, Modulation Chorus at
low depth. Automate Feedback upward on the phrase you want to run away.

**Chorus, not delay.** Delay at its minimum, Feedback 0, Mix 50%, Modulation
Chorus, Mod Depth 25 to 40%. The bucket-brigade filtering makes this darker
than a digital chorus.

**True vibrato.** Delay at its minimum, Feedback 0, Mix 100%, Modulation
Vibrato, Mod Rate around 5 Hz. Full depth is a real one-semitone wobble. 50%
is a singer's.

**Behind the beat.** Sync, 1/4, Nudge +4 to +8%. The repeats sit lagged behind
the grid like a tape echo running slightly slow. Automate Nudge back to 0 on
the turnaround and the groove tightens on cue.

**The gesture.** Set a long delay with high feedback, then grab the Delay knob
and move it while the repeats are sounding. That pitch bend is the reason this
plugin exists.

title: Manual > Amnesia > Notes > The idea
text:
Before delay was digital, it was a line of buckets. A bucket-brigade device
passes an analog voltage from one capacitor to the next in step with a clock,
thousands of stages deep. Out the far end comes your signal: late, darker than
it went in, a little noisier, and slightly wrong in a way that turned out to be
the point. Repeats decay into mush instead of decaying into silence.

Amnesia models two 4096-stage bucket-brigade chips in series, with the
companding noise reduction, clock-tracking filters and soft-limited feedback
that surrounded them.

**The part worth knowing:** on real hardware the delay time is the clock speed.
Changing the delay time changes the playback rate of everything already in the
line, so the echoes bend in pitch as the knob moves. That slew is modeled here.
It is why **Delay** is a continuous, automatable knob rather than a list of
times. Turning it is a performance gesture. Automate it.

title: Manual > Amnesia > Notes > The three time sources
text:
The `TEMPO` rail selects who sets the time: `MANUAL`, `TAP` or `SYNC`. The big
knob is always live. What changes is its job.

**Manual** is the default. The knob is the time. Tap Divide is grayed out
because nothing is feeding it a tempo.

**Tap.** Click the `TAP` cell twice or more. The interval between clicks is the
tempo, and Tap Divide picks the note value. The tapped tempo is remembered.
Change the subdivision later, or reopen the session, and it re-resolves.

**Sync.** Locks to your host's tempo times Tap Divide. The plugin never writes
the Delay parameter in this mode, so it will not fight your host automation.

**In Tap and Sync the knob becomes `NUDGE`**: plus or minus 33.3% around the
resolved time, for push and pull against the beat. A few percent sits the
repeats behind the groove or leans them ahead. The far ends reach real rhythmic
ground: +33% of an eighth is a quarter-triplet. Double-click to land on the
grid. Nudge slews the pitch as it moves, like the Delay knob, and it is
automatable. A clip envelope or LFO on Nudge breathes against the grid without
losing it. The display keeps showing the true resolved time in ms. The result
is capped at 1.5 s, so pushing a long delay longer eventually flattens out; the
ms readout shows the truth. Click `MANUAL` to leave. The effective time is
carried onto the Delay knob, so nothing jumps.

title: Manual > Amnesia > Notes > Tap 2, the stereo image
text:
**Mono** is the same echo on both sides, as it always was. Any note value is a
second tap. There is one delay line. Tap 1 is on the left at the delay time,
recirculating as usual. Tap 2 is on the right at this note value, a single tap
that does not feed back. The right side hears the same decaying train, starting
at its own time. Dry stays where it was. In Tap and Sync the value is an
independent subdivision of the same tempo (Triplet applies, and Nudge moves it
with tap 1). In Manual there is no tempo, so the positions read as a ratio
against Delay: x1.5, x1, x.75, x.5, x.25, with x1 as unison. Like Delay it is
capped at 1.5 s. On a mono track there is no right side, so it stays Mono. The
hardware had one output; this image is ours.

title: Manual > Amnesia > Notes > Feedback and modulation
text:
Sustained bass regenerates earlier on the Feedback dial than percussive
material does. That is the compander doing its job, not a fault.

On the hardware the modulation rate was fixed per mode. Here it is yours. Mod
Depth is calibrated by measurement: Chorus at 1 Hz spans up to about a
quarter-semitone of shimmer, and Vibrato at 5 Hz reaches a true one-semitone
wobble at full depth. Depth is zero by default.

title: Manual > Fifty-Fifty
text: A Japanese half-track stereo reel-to-reel tape machine.

title: Manual > Fifty-Fifty > Controls
text:
| Control | Range | Default | What it does |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Speed** | 15 IPS · 7.5 IPS | 15 IPS | The main tone control. 15 runs brighter, with a higher, bigger low-end bump. 7.5 has a lower, tighter bump and rolls off earlier up top. |
| **EQ** | NAB · IEC | NAB | Which standard the machine is aligned to. NAB drives the bottom onto the tape harder, so it saturates sooner. IEC reads leaner and cleaner down low. See *Notes*. |
| **Input** | -24 to +24 dB | 0.0 | Record level: how hard you hit the oxide. It drives saturation and changes level, like a deck's record gain. |
| **Bias** | -100 to +100 | 0 | Under-biased at the negative end: brighter, dirtier, noisier. Over-biased at the positive end: rolled-off top, cleaner. Zero is aligned. |
| **Head Bump** | 0 to 100% | 33 | Depth of the low-frequency head resonance. 100 is the real machine, about +2.1 dB at 40 Hz on NAB at 15 IPS, tapering out by 100 Hz. See *Notes*. |
| **Flutter** | 0 to 100% | 15 | Wow and flutter depth. This is a good transport, so the default is subtle. It is not a lo-fi wobble effect. |
| **Mix** | 0 to 100% | 100 | Parallel tape. |
| **Output** | -24 to +24 dB | 0.0 | Trim, to level-match against Input drive. |
| **Auto Gain** | off · on | off | Matches output loudness to input, so an A/B compares tone rather than level. No latency; settles over about 3 s. Dims **Output** while on. See *Controls every plugin shares*. |

title: Manual > Fifty-Fifty > Readings
text:
TAPE RESPONSE
:   Magnitude against frequency, in dB relative to 1 kHz: the head bump at the
    bottom, the speed-dependent loss at the top, and the NAB/IEC shelf. It is
    measured by running the real tape machine, configured as your audio path is.
    Speed, EQ, Bias, Head Bump and Mix all move it.

    The amber curve is the machine you are on. The faint one behind it is the
    other tape speed at otherwise identical settings, so what Speed costs you
    is visible rather than described.

OUTPUT
:   The arc on the right is the plugin's output level, with the last few dB
    before clipping marked at the top of the scale. In the plugin's own look
    the arc is a tape reel that turns while the transport runs, with the output
    level printed in its header.

Two things worth knowing about the response curve:

- **It tracks how hard you are driving it,** and the level it was measured at
  is printed in the header. This machine has no level-independent response.
  The record and reproduce EQ only cancel because the tape itself compresses,
  so a single curve would only ever have been true at one operating point.
  Push it and you will watch the head bump flatten. That is the plugin's
  character, drawn rather than described.
- **Flutter is left out on purpose.** It is a modulation in time. It would
  smear a static magnitude measurement, and it has nothing meaningful to draw
  on a frequency axis. The Flutter knob is not broken when the curve ignores
  it.

title: Manual > Fifty-Fifty > Starting points
text:
**Mix bus glue.** 15 IPS, NAB, Input +2 to +4, Head Bump at default, Flutter
10 to 15%. Trim back with Output and A/B.

**Weight on a thin mix.** 7.5 IPS, NAB, Head Bump 70 to 100. The lower
resonance fills in the bottom. 100 is the machine as it was.

**Drive, on purpose.** Input +8 or more, Bias negative for brightness and dirt.
Best on a drum bus or a single source, not a master.

**Just the softening.** Input 0, Head Bump 0, Flutter 0, Mix 100%. What is left
is the record and reproduce curves and the hysteresis. It is the subtlest
useful setting in the plugin.

title: Manual > Fifty-Fifty > Notes > The idea
text:
Most tape plugins are, quietly, transformer plugins. The machines they model
were built around input and output transformers, and a large share of the
"tape" sound people reach for is iron.

The deck this one models has none. It is a Japanese half-track studio machine.
Its signal path is transformerless and direct-coupled, so everything you hear
is tape: the magnetic hysteresis of the oxide, the bias, the record and
reproduce equalization curves, the low-frequency resonance where the head gap
meets the tape, and the small speed instabilities of a real transport. Nothing
is standing in for it.

That negative constraint is the whole product. If you want transformer color,
that is Remanence's job, and you can stack the two. Here you get tape and only
tape, which is cleaner and more open than most tape emulation.

title: Manual > Fifty-Fifty > Notes > Bus or track
text:
The voicing is taken from the half-track stereo version of the machine: two
tracks across the full width of quarter-inch tape, running in one direction,
which is the format studios mixed to. That is the cleanest configuration the
deck came in, and it is why this sits well across a mix.

**It is not only a bus plugin.** The same machine shipped as a multitrack, with
the same heads and the same audio electronics, and studios ran everything
through it a track at a time. An instance on a single source is as faithful to
the hardware as one on the two-bus. Tape saturation stacks the way it did on a
real multitrack, so a little on each of several tracks lands somewhere
different from a lot on the master. Both are worth trying.

title: Manual > Fifty-Fifty > Notes > How to drive it
text:
Input is the control that matters and the one most likely to be misused. At 0
the plugin is aligned and close to clean, with distortion in the fractions of
a percent, the figure a well-aligned deck hit. Distortion rises steeply as you
push past that. That is faithful, and it means small Input moves have large
consequences. Use Output to match levels while you audition. Otherwise you will
prefer whichever version is louder.

Speed and EQ are not subtle, and they are not quality settings. 7.5 IPS is not
worse than 15. It is a different low end. Try both before touching anything
else.

title: Manual > Fifty-Fifty > Notes > The head bump, and the two standards
text:
Engineers who used these decks describe the head bump as something you learn
to work around. So the Head Bump knob reaches the machine at its top, and the
default sits at a third of it.

**Head Bump at zero is not a flat low end either, just a different shape.** With
the knob all the way down, the chain reads about -0.4 dB at 40 Hz and falls
away below that. What is left is the subsonic filter every tape chain needs,
not a tone control. The head resonance is the only thing lifting the low end
here, so the knob takes you from the machine down to something flatter than
the machine ever was.

**NAB and IEC differ in how the bottom behaves, not just how much there is.**
NAB pre-emphasizes the low end onto the tape and removes it again on playback.
So the bottom octave arrives at the oxide several dB hot and saturates before
anything else does. That is why bass on a NAB-aligned deck thickens as you push
it. IEC sends it through flat. Expect similar amounts of low end from both, and
different behavior when you drive them.

title: Manual > Jointer
text: A clipper that clips the waveform your listener hears.

title: Manual > Jointer > Controls
text:
| Control | Range | Default | What it does |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Drive** | 0 to +24 dB | 0.0 | Level into the ceiling. This is the amount-of-clipping control. |
| **Ceiling** | -12 to 0 dB | -1.00 | Where the top is. See *Notes* for why the default is -1.0 rather than -0.1. |
| **Margin** | 0 to 1.00 dB | 0.30 | How far under the Ceiling the plugin lands, as insurance against anything downstream. See *Notes*. |
| **Knee** | 0 to 24 dB | 0.0 | 0 is a hard corner. Higher values start the shaping further below the ceiling, so the clip becomes a soft curve rather than a wall. |
| **Asym** | -100 to +100% | 0 | Moves the knee between the two halves of the waveform. A curve that treats the two halves differently adds even harmonics. 0 is the symmetric curve. See *Notes*. |
| **Mix** | 0 to 100% | 100 | Parallel clipping. The ceiling is applied again after the blend, so turning Mix down cannot defeat the number on the panel. |
| **Compensate** | off · on | off | Shortens a soft knee so it reaches the ceiling at an input of the ceiling. This recovers the level a soft knee lands under, without driving harder. Dimmed at Knee 0, where there is no knee to shorten. See *Notes*. |
| **Stereo Link** | off · on | on | Lit, both channels are driven by the same amount. Off, they clip independently, which shifts the stereo image on the transients where clipping engages. Dimmed and inactive on a mono track. |
| **Oversampling** | 4X · 8X · 16X | 8X | How finely the between-sample waveform is resolved. There is no OFF; see *Controls every plugin shares*. |

title: Manual > Jointer > Controls
text:
Latency is about 1.6 ms at 44.1 kHz and 8x. It is reported to your DAW and
compensated automatically.

**A soft Knee will not reach your Ceiling on transients, and that is not a
fault.** The curve only arrives at the ceiling once the input is well past it.
At Knee 12 you need about +3.5 dBFS going in, at Knee 24 about +4.4. So gentle
settings land under the target unless you drive hard. There is a second effect.
Clipping happens inside the oversampled section, and the signal is then
band-limited on the way back down, which lowers the peak of impulsive material.
Measured on impulses, that is roughly 0.9 dB under the ceiling at Knee 0 and
1.5 dB under at Knee 6. Drums and percussion with a soft knee will read
comfortably below the number you set. To reach the ceiling, drive harder, use a
harder knee, or switch on Compensate. Compensate has its own section under
*Notes*.

title: Manual > Jointer > Readings
text:
The four large figures are what came out. The two in the row just above the
knobs restate what your knobs are set to, not what the plugin cost you. The rows
below them are the cost.

TRUE PEAK
:   The true peak of the output. It sits next to `SAMPLE PEAK` on purpose. On
    unclipped material the two differ by a few tenths of a dB, and the busier
    and louder the master, the wider that gap gets. If it ever turns red, the
    output exceeded the ceiling target. That should not happen; please report
    it.

SAMPLE PEAK
:   The highest sample of the output. This is the figure every other meter you
    own reads.

SHORT TERM
:   Short-term loudness, because that is what a mastering decision turns on.

INTEGRATED LUFS
:   Integrated loudness over the whole pass, in LUFS (loudness units relative to
    full scale), for the same reason.

DRIVEN PEAK
:   The true peak going into the shaping curve: your input plus Drive. It tells
    you how hard you are pushing at the ceiling.

CEILING TARGET
:   Where the plugin is aiming: your Ceiling setting minus Margin. With the
    defaults it reads -1.30 dBTP (decibels true peak). If the true peak figure
    looks like an undershoot, this is why. It is stated rather than hidden. A
    plugin whose pitch is that its numbers are true cannot have a knob that
    quietly means something else.

LOUDNESS ADDED
:   How much louder engaging the plugin made the material, in LU (loudness
    units). Drive is inside this comparison, so it answers the question you
    have: is this worth what it cost?

title: Manual > Jointer > Readings
text:
DISTORTION ADDED
:   The difference between what went into the clipping curve and what came out,
    as a percentage. It is not labeled THD (total harmonic distortion) on
    purpose. Clipping is the only nonlinearity here, so the difference signal is
    the distortion. But it is a THD+N-shaped figure rather than a harmonic sum,
    and calling it THD would claim more precision than it has.

SAMPLES CLIPPED
:   What fraction of samples the curve touched.

TP REDUCTION
:   How far the true peak came down: `DRIVEN PEAK` minus the `TRUE PEAK` at the
    top. That is the peak the clipping curve removed, and you can check the
    subtraction by eye. It can read negative with Compensate on; see *Notes*.

CLAMP CAUGHT
:   How much the final true-peak clamp had to do after the shaping curve. This
    is the work the curve did not already do. Small numbers are normal. Large
    ones mean Drive is asking for more than the curve can absorb, and the clamp
    is holding the ceiling on its own.

RESET
:   The peak and loudness figures are max-hold. They accumulate over the whole
    pass rather than tracking the moment. `RESET` clears them.

The small plot inside the report draws the curve your Knee and Asym settings
make, against the ceiling target. When Asym is off center, the negative half's
curve is drawn faintly beside it, so you can see both corners. In the clip trace
on the right, a red line along the top of the input marks every stretch where
the clipper took something off.

title: Manual > Jointer > Starting points
text:
**Streaming master.** Load the **Streaming (-1.0 dBTP)** preset, leave Margin
at 0.30, and bring Drive up until `LOUDNESS ADDED` reads what you want to spend.
Watch `DISTORTION ADDED` as you go. On dense material it climbs faster than it
sounds like it should.

**CD or DDP.** Load **CD / DDP (-0.1 dBTP)**. If you are already working at
44.1 kHz and the file leaves this plugin ready to burn, take Margin to 0. The
whole point of -0.1 is the last tenth of a dB, and there is nothing downstream
to protect against.

**Clip before a limiter.** Drive up until `SAMPLES CLIPPED` is a few percent,
Knee 0, Ceiling wherever the limiter's input wants it. Taking the sharpest
transients off with a clipper first gives the limiter less to grab at, and the
two together stay cleaner than either pushed alone.

**Drum bus.** Knee 3 to 6 dB, Mix 70 to 80%, Drive high. The knee keeps it from
sounding like a wall, and the parallel path keeps the stick attack while the
clipper handles the body.

**Just a safety net.** Drive 0, Knee 0, Margin 0.30, Ceiling at your delivery
value. It does nothing until something crosses the line, and then it catches
it. The damage report tells you afterwards whether anything did.

title: Manual > Jointer > Notes > The idea
text:
Digital meters lie by omission. A meter reads samples, but a converter does not
play samples. It reconstructs a continuous waveform through them, and that
waveform routinely rises higher than any individual sample. A master that reads
exactly 0.0 dBFS on every meter you own can still overload the converter in
someone's phone. It will do so on the loudest moments, which are the ones you
cared about most.

Jointer clips that reconstructed waveform, the one your listener hears, rather
than the samples. That is the whole product.

The name is the operation. A jointer plane is long so that it rides the high
spots. It takes down only what stands proud of the reference, passes over the
hollows, and stops when the surface is true. That is what happens here. What
exceeds the ceiling comes off, and material that never reached it is left
alone. A thickness planer, the other tool people compare it to, does the
opposite: it takes a uniform cut off everything to hit a dimension. That is not
how this works. A jointer's job is also to make a surface **true**, which is
what a true-peak ceiling is.

Everything else on the panel exists to tell you what it cost. A clipper is a
destructive process, and most of them ask you to trust that the destruction was
tasteful. This one prints the receipt: distortion added, samples clipped,
loudness gained, and the true and sample peaks side by side. The gap between
those two peaks is the reason this plugin exists, so it is shown rather than
left to theory.

title: Manual > Jointer > Notes > Asym
text:
At +100 the positive half of the waveform gets a knee twice as deep as Knee, and
the negative half clips hard. At -100 it is the reverse. A curve that treats the
two halves differently adds even harmonics, which is the part of a FET's
(field-effect transistor's) character you hear. 0 is the symmetric curve. It
shapes only the moments when the signal is over the knee, and like any
asymmetric clipper it leaves a little DC in those moments.

title: Manual > Jointer > Notes > Compensate: reaching the ceiling without driving harder
text:
A soft knee lands under your ceiling. At Knee 6, a peak driven to exactly the
ceiling comes out 1.16 dB below it. At Knee 12 it is 1.80 dB below. The curve
does not arrive at the ceiling until the input is well past it. That is a
property of the knee's shape, and it can be fixed by changing the shape. That is
all Compensate does.

A knee has a start, which you set with Knee, and a span: how far above that
start the curve keeps bending before it goes flat. With Compensate off, that
span always runs to well above your ceiling. With it on, the span is shortened
so the curve goes flat exactly at the ceiling. Same starting point, same
rounded corner, but it commits to the ceiling sooner.

**There is no gain stage.** Nothing is turned up after the clipper. The level
comes from the curve itself rising a little faster through the corner, up to
one and a third times as fast at the steepest point. That is the only place
missing peak can come from. It is also why **`TP REDUCTION` can read a negative
number**: on a peak that lands inside the knee, the plugin added level rather
than removing it. The readout is allowed to say so.

Here is what a peak driven to exactly your ceiling comes out at:

| Knee | Compensate off | Compensate on |
|:--|:--|:--|
| 3 dB | 0.66 dB under | at the ceiling |
| 6 dB | 1.16 dB under | at the ceiling |
| 12 dB | 1.80 dB under | at the ceiling |
| 24 dB | 2.32 dB under | at the ceiling |

**On real music the difference is larger than a peak reading suggests.** The
same mix, Ceiling -1.0, Knee 12, Drive +3, measured both ways:

title: Manual > Jointer > Notes > Compensate: reaching the ceiling without driving harder
text:
| | Compensate off | Compensate on |
|:--|:--|:--|
| True peak out | **-1.60 dBTP** | **-0.98 dBTP** |
| Loudness added | 1.72 LU | **3.83 LU** |
| Distortion added | 18.8% | 21.1% |

Two thirds of a dB of peak, and over two LU of loudness, from a knee shape
rather than from more clipping. The proportion of samples in the shaping region
is identical in both columns, because the knee still starts in the same place.

**The cost is not only "more distortion".** At Knee 12 above, distortion
rises, because the compensated curve goes flat at the ceiling instead of
bending past it, so material driven above the ceiling meets a harder corner.
But at Knee 6 on the same mix, distortion fell from 12.2% to 10.3% while
loudness still rose. There, the compensated curve sits closer to the input
through the region where most samples land, so it deviates from them less.
Which way it goes depends on your knee, your drive and your material. Watch
`DISTORTION ADDED` and decide by ear.

Two things Compensate does not do. It does not touch anything below the knee
start, which stays bit-for-bit unaltered either way. And it does not address
the second effect above, band-limiting lowering the peaks of impulsive
material, because that happens after the shaping curve, where no change of
shape can reach it. Drums with a soft knee will still read a little under.

It is off by default, and dimmed at Knee 0, where there is no knee to shorten.

title: Manual > Jointer > Notes > Why the ceiling defaults to -1.0 dBTP and not -0.1
text:
-0.1 is honest here. The plugin holds it, which is not true of every clipper.
But it is a CD and DDP value, not a safe default. Lossy encoders do not preserve
peaks. A file sitting at -0.1 dBTP can come out of AAC, Ogg or MP3 encoding
above full scale and clip the listener's decoder. That is the same failure as
an intersample over, one step further down the chain. -1.0 is the only common
ceiling that survives the trip. Both ship as factory presets, named for the
delivery they suit. A third preset, **Drum Bus Shave**, is not a delivery
setting. It pushes 6 dB of Drive into a 6 dB Knee: the clipper used as a sound.

title: Manual > Jointer > Notes > Put it last, at the rate you are delivering
text:
A true-peak ceiling is only valid at the sample rate it was applied at. If you
clip in a 96 or 88.2 kHz session and then convert the master down to 44.1 or 48,
the conversion moves the peaks and the ceiling no longer holds. Put Jointer last
in the chain, at the rate you are delivering.

This is not a rounding error. On a real master clipped to -1.0 dBTP in an 88.2
kHz session, converting to 48 kHz took the true peak up to **-0.79 dBTP**. That
is 0.26 dB above a ceiling that had held exactly.

The reason is specific to clipping. Flattening a peak requires harmonics above
the audio band, and those harmonics are what holds the peak down. Anything
downstream that band-limits the signal removes them, and the peak springs back
up. A sample-rate conversion, a delivery encode, and the listener's own
reconstruction all do this. A compressor or limiter does not have this problem,
because riding gain barely widens the spectrum. It is the price of clipping
specifically.

**Margin is the insurance.** It lands the output a set distance under your
Ceiling, so there is somewhere for the peaks to spring back into. The 0.30 dB
default covers the worst case measured so far, with a little room. If your
chain ends at Jointer, meaning you are clipping at the delivery rate and nothing
downstream touches the file, set it to 0 and take the level back.

title: Manual > Firmament
text: A plate reverb, solved from the physics of the sheet rather than sampled.

title: Manual > Firmament > Controls
text:
| Control | Range | Default | What it does |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Size** | Large · Medium · Small · Mini | Large | Rebuilds the plate. Large is the classic 2 x 1 meter unit; Mini is 27 x 29 cm, the real foil unit's dimensions. What your ear hears is area. A smaller plate has fewer, more widely spaced modes, so it sounds brighter and more metallic. |
| **Thickness** | Plate · Foil | Plate | Plate is 0.5 mm, the classic steel plate. Foil is 18 microns, the gold-foil unit. Each carries its own measured decay curve. See *Notes*. |
| **Material** | Steel · Alum · Copper · Silver · Gold | Steel | Also rebuilds the plate. The list runs bright to dark. Steel is the reference machine. Gold is the darkest, and the one no real studio had in a full-size plate. See *Notes*. |
| **Low Cut** | Off · -4 · -12 · -24 dB | -4 | A cut at 100 Hz on the way into the plate, matching the switch on the real drive amplifier. With Makeup off it only cuts, and never gets louder. See *Notes*. |
| **Makeup** (on Low Cut) | off · on | off | Holds the reverb's level through the Low Cut switch, solved for a bass-heavy source. On a snare or a guitar it adds level the cut never removed, up to 12 dB at -24. See *Notes*. |
| **Modes** | Eco · Mid · Full | Mid | How many resonators run. This is a CPU control, not a quality ladder. See *Notes*. |
| **Pre-Delay** | 0 to 250 ms | 0.0 | Delays the reverb only. The dry stays where the host put it. |
| **Drive** | 0 to 100% | 0 | The drive amplifier's tube stage, pushed past the level the plate was specified at. Level-compensated, so it changes the tone of what reaches the plate, not the volume. 0 is the machine as specified, with the stage out of the circuit. |
| **Decay** | 1.0 to 4.0 s | 2.0 | Reverberation time measured at 500 Hz, which is how plates have always been specified. The range is the real machine's published one. The low end will be much longer than the number. |
| **Compress** | off · on | off | The drive amplifier's own compressor, 2:1 above -18 dBFS. On the hardware it stops the exciter being overdriven, so it catches peaks rather than gluing. Level-compensated, so switching it on changes the dynamics and not the volume. |
| **Mix** | 0 to 100% | 30 | Equal-power, so the total stays steady as you sweep rather than dipping in the middle. |
| **Output** | -24 to +24 dB | 0.0 | Final trim, applied after the mix. |
| **Auto Gain** | off · on | off | Matches output loudness to input, so an A/B compares tone rather than level. No latency; settles over about 3 s. Dims **Output** while on. See *Controls every plugin shares*. |

title: Manual > Firmament > Controls
text:
In the plugin's own look, Decay is the plate's damping wheel rather than a knob:
a needle over a printed scale, read in seconds, dragged like a knob. In Classic
it is a knob.

**Size, Thickness and Material combine into a machine.** All three feed the same
number, the plate's bending stiffness, so no one of them alone picks a real
unit. The classic 140 is Large + Plate + Steel. The gold foil is Mini + Foil +
Gold. Mini + Plate + Steel is a good small plate, but no such machine was ever
built. The factory presets set all three, so use those if you want the real
thing rather than a plausible one.

title: Manual > Firmament > Readings
text:
DECAY TIME (s) vs FREQUENCY (Hz)
:   The curve on the right of the panel is decay time against frequency. Gray
    is the longest decay the plate can produce; amber is the current setting.
    On a steel plate it is not a flat tail, and it is not supposed to be. Switch
    between Plate and Foil at the same Decay and watch the gray line change
    shape.

MODES
:   Bottom right of the curve display: the number of resonators running now. It
    is live and measured rather than estimated, so the answer for your machine
    is on the panel.

CPU
:   What share of one CPU core the resonators are using, measured, beside the
    count. Shown only while audio is running. If it is close to 100%, that is
    the number to act on; see *Notes*.

COMP
:   The drive amplifier's compressor at work, in dB, while Compress is on and
    audio is running.

> **Click any caption (`SIZE`, `THICKNESS`, `MATERIAL`, `MODES`) to switch the
> whole panel between names and measurements.** Size becomes area in square
> meters. Material becomes the plate's wave speed in meters per second.
> Thickness becomes 0.5 mm and 18 µm. Modes becomes the per-Bark resonator cap.
> Click again to go back. It is worth doing once even if you never use it
> again. It shows that Steel and Alum are 5288 and 5394 m/s, so nearly the same
> plate that the difference between them is small, while Gold sits down at
> 2253.

title: Manual > Firmament > Starting points
text:
**Start from a real machine.** Five of the presets are documented settings
rather than tastes. *140 Plate*, *140 Damper Closed* and *140 Damper Open* are
the steel plate at the bottom, middle and top of its published reverb-time
range. *240 Gold Foil* and *240 Foil + 262* are the foil, the second with the
compressor engaged, because the real foil unit's companding shortened its decay
by about a tenth.

Those presets set Size, Thickness and Material together, which matters. All
three feed the same number, so no one of them alone picks a real unit. Mini on
its own is not the foil machine. It is the 240's dimensions in half-millimeter
steel, a small plate nobody ever built. Fine if you want it, but it is not the
machine.

**Vocal plate.** Large, Plate, Steel, Decay 1.8 to 2.2 s, Pre-Delay 20 to 40
ms, Mix 20 to 30%. The pre-delay keeps the words in front of the reverb.

**Snare.** Medium, Plate, Steel, Decay 1.2 to 1.6 s, Pre-Delay 0, Mix 25 to
40%. Short and bright, the sound plates were bought for.

**Drums without the boom.** Mini, Foil, Gold, Decay 1.5 to 2.5 s, Low Cut Off,
Mix 25 to 40%. The foil's flat low end means you can leave the cut alone and
still not lose the kick. The tail is not down there. This is what the real 240
was bought for.

**Wash.** Large, Plate, Gold, Decay 3.5 to 4.0 s, Low Cut -24, Mix 50% or
more. Gold is dense and dark, and at long decays the low end needs the deeper
cut.

title: Manual > Firmament > Starting points
text:
**Something metallic and small.** Small, Plate, Aluminum, Decay 1.0 to 1.4 s.
Fewer, more separated modes. This is where the plate stops being a
general-purpose reverb and becomes an effect.

**If it sounds boomy,** reach for Low Cut before Decay. The bottom of a plate
rings far longer than the middle, so the fix is usually to stop exciting it
down there rather than to shorten the whole tail. Switching to Foil is the
other answer, and a more drastic one. It changes the machine rather than
filtering it.

title: Manual > Firmament > Notes > The idea
text:
Most plate reverbs are either a recording of a plate or an arrangement of
delays tuned until it sounds like one. This is neither. It solves the physics
of a particular sheet of metal: its resonant modes, their frequencies, how long
each one rings, and how strongly each is heard at two pickup positions. Then it
runs those thousands of resonators live.

That matters for one practical reason. A recording of a plate is a snapshot of
one plate at one setting. You can filter it afterwards, but you cannot change
what it is. Here the plate is described rather than captured, so **Size,
Thickness and Material are not tone controls. They rebuild the instrument.**
Gold is not a darker preset. It is what a plate of that density and stiffness
would do, including plates nobody ever built, because you cannot record a gold
plate that does not exist.

The name is the same idea. "Firmament" comes, through Greek and Latin, from a
Hebrew word for a thing beaten out into a thin sheet, the verb used of
hammering gold into plating. A plate reverb is a sheet of steel half a
millimeter thick, hung under tension in a frame. The word is the object. With
Thickness set to Foil it is the object twice over, because the other machine
modeled here is eighteen microns of beaten gold.

title: Manual > Firmament > Notes > What a plate does
text:
Two things surprise people coming from room and hall reverbs. Both are correct,
not faults.

**There is no early reflection pattern, and there is no direct sound.** A room
gives you the source, then distinct early reflections, then a tail. A plate
smears everything at once. The vibration spreads across the sheet at different
speeds for different frequencies, so nothing arrives cleanly. What you hear as
