the direct sound is your dry signal and nothing else. That is why Mix matters
more here than on a room. The dry path is the only dry there is.

**The low end rings much longer than the top.** On the real machine the damper
plate has strong control below about 2 kHz and almost none above 5 kHz. A
setting that gives two seconds at 500 Hz can give ten or more at 50 Hz. The
curve on the right of the panel shows this. The gray line is the longest decay
available; the amber line is where you are now. It is not a flat tail, and it
is not supposed to be.

**Unless you switch to Foil, where it is.** The gold foil machine's measured
decay is nearly flat below 1 kHz, with about the same reverb time at 80 Hz as
at 500 Hz. The steel plate's climbs steeply there. That one difference is most
of what people mean when they say the foil does not boom. It is why the two
carry separate measured curves rather than one curve with a tilt on it. Switch
between Plate and Foil at the same Decay and watch the gray line change shape.

title: Manual > Firmament > Notes > Size, Thickness and Material
text:
What your ear hears in Size is **area**, because modal density depends on area
alone. A smaller plate has fewer, more widely spaced modes, so it sounds
brighter and more metallic.

There are only two Thicknesses, because each carries its own **measured** decay
curve, and those are the only two ever published. The difference is not subtle.
A plate's decay rises steeply into the bass. A foil's is flat below 1 kHz,
which is why the 240 is prized for not booming.

Of the Materials, Steel is the reference machine. Aluminum is nearly identical;
its wave speed is within 2% of steel's. Copper and silver are denser. Gold is
the darkest, and the one no real studio had in a full-size plate.

title: Manual > Firmament > Notes > Low Cut, and its Makeup
text:
The Low Cut switch exists because over-exciting a plate at low frequencies is
the main thing that makes it distort. A modeled plate is bottom-heavy for the
same reason a real one is. With Makeup off (the default) the switch only cuts.
On bass-heavy material the tail gets a little quieter as you cut. On a snare or
a guitar it barely moves. It never gets louder.

Makeup holds the reverb's level through the switch, solved for a bass-heavy
source. On a full mix it does what it says. On a snare or a guitar, which lose
almost nothing to the cut, it adds level the cut never removed, up to 12 dB at
-24. Sessions saved before this option existed load with it on, so they sound
as they did.

title: Manual > Firmament > Notes > Drive is the amplifier, not the plate
text:
The plate itself is a clean device, specified under 1% distortion at any
output level. The drive amplifier in front of it carries a compressor and a
bass cut to keep it there. Drive pushes that amplifier's tube stage past where
it was aligned, so what reaches the plate is brighter and harder, and the plate
rings on that. With Compress on, the amp is held back and Drive bites later, as
on the hardware. The stage sits where the amplifier does, before the
pre-emphasis that stands for the driver coil, so the whole program drives it.
The low end is what pushes a tube hardest. The harmonics it makes pass the
pre-emphasis into the plate, while the fundamentals that made them are still
held back. A pushed plate amp goes dense and forward, not muddy.

title: Manual > Firmament > Notes > On a mono track, pick the mono/stereo variant
text:
Pro Tools lists Firmament as **(mono)** and **(mono/stereo)** on a mono track;
Logic as **Mono** and **Mono→Stereo**. The second one is the plate. The drive
is one channel on the real machine too, and the stereo is made by two pickups
at different distances from it. The plain mono variant sums those pickups to
one channel, and is only for a track that must stay mono. On a stereo track
there is one variant, and it is already stereo. The input is summed before the
plate, as the hardware does, and the two pickups spread it back out.

title: Manual > Firmament > Notes > Modes: what the setting costs
text:
This is the only control that trades computation for sound, so it is worth
being plain about what it buys.

A real plate's frequency response is not smooth. It has a measured ripple of
about 10 dB between its peaks and dips, and that unevenness is a large part of
what a plate sounds like. More resonators make the response smoother.

| Setting | Resonators | Ripple | CPU |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Eco** | ~3,400 | 11.8 dB | lowest |
| **Mid** | ~5,400 | 10.5 dB | about half of Full |
| **Full** | ~8,600 | 9.7 dB | highest |

**Mid is the default because it is the closest to a real plate, not because it
is a compromise.** Full is smoother than the machine it models. Eco is
noticeably rougher, and is there for sessions running several instances. If you
can hear a difference between Mid and Full on your material, use whichever you
prefer. But Full is not the "correct" setting, and Mid is not a reduced one.

**Those resonator counts are for a steel plate.** Size, Thickness and Material
all change how many resonators a given setting produces, and Thickness changes
it most. Measured on this machine at Mid:

| Machine | Resonators |
|:--|:--|
| Large + Steel + Plate (the 140) | 5,413 |
| Mini + Gold + Foil (the 240) | 7,443 |
| Large + Gold + Foil (never existed) | 6,528 |

title: Manual > Firmament > Notes > Modes: what the setting costs
text:
**Foil costs roughly a third more CPU than Plate at the same Modes setting.** A
foil's modes are packed far more densely: the 240 has 3.3 per Hz against a
140's 1.3. So more of the budget is spent low down, where a plate hardly needs
any. If you are running several instances, that is the setting to watch, and
dropping Foil to Eco costs less than you would expect.

**At the larger sizes a foil is an approximation rather than a solve.** A 2 x 1
meter sheet of 18-micron gold would have 85 modes per Hz. That is tens of
thousands of resonators below 1 kHz alone, more than any plugin can run. Those
sizes thin the low end to fit, so they keep the foil's character and its full
frequency range, but not its true low-frequency resolution. Both real machines,
the 140 at Large and the 240 at Mini, are comfortably inside the budget and are
modeled without any thinning of that kind.

The readout under the curve is live and measured rather than estimated, so the
answer for your machine is on the panel.

title: Manual > Firmament > Notes > Modes and sample rate
text:
**Your session's sample rate multiplies all of this, and it is the thing most
likely to catch you out.** The cost is per sample. A 96 kHz session costs
close to twice a 48 kHz one at the same setting. That is measured, and
linear, with no surprise threshold in between. Working at 88.2 or 96 kHz
therefore moves Full to roughly where two instances of it would sit at 44.1.

That combination, Full at a high sample rate with a Foil, which is a third more
again, is the most expensive thing this plugin can be asked to do. On a current
machine it is comfortable. On an older one it may want more than a whole CPU
core. A plugin that cannot finish a block in time is heard as clicks and
dropouts, not as something running slowly. On Windows and Intel Macs, a
processor from roughly 2013 on (one with AVX2) runs the resonators several
times faster than an older one does, so the oldest machines are the ones to
watch.

**You do not have to estimate any of this.** The share of a core is on the
panel, live, next to the resonator count. If it is close to 100%, that is the
number to act on:

- **Drop Modes to Mid.** It is the default, the closest of the three to a real
  plate, and about half the cost of Full.
- **Drop to Eco** if you are running several instances. It is rougher, and on a
  reverb that is often inaudible in a full mix.
- **Or put the reverb on a send** rather than on several channels. That is how
  a real plate was used: one machine, many sources.

title: Manual > Firmament > Notes > Modes and sample rate
text:
Little of this applies to the rest of the line. Undercroft is the only other
plugin with a cost worth watching, and it prints its own on its display. The
others are a rounding error next to these two.

title: Manual > Keelson
text: A bus compressor with switchable output iron.

title: Manual > Keelson > Controls
text:
| Control | Range | Default | What it does |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Threshold** | -40 to 0 dB | -16 | Where compression starts. Watch the meter rather than the number. On a mix bus, 2 to 4 dB of reduction on the loudest parts is usually plenty. |
| **Ratio** | 2:1 · 4:1 · 10:1 | 2:1 | A stepped knob, not a sweep, because the hardware's positions are part of what it is. 2:1 is the glue setting and where most mixes want it. 10:1 is for compression that is meant to be heard. |
| **Attack** | 0.1 · 0.3 · 1 · 3 · 10 · 30 ms | 10 | Stepped, like Ratio and Release. The slow end is the point: at 30 ms, transients pass through untouched and only what follows is compressed. See *Notes*. |
| **Release** | 0.1 · 0.3 · 0.6 · 1.2 s · AUTO | AUTO | Fixed times, plus the program-dependent AUTO. Start on AUTO. See *Notes*. |
| **SC HPF** | 20 to 185 Hz | 20 = off | A highpass on the *detector only*; the audio is never filtered. Stops the kick drum from deciding the compression for the whole mix. Try 60 to 100 Hz if the low end is pumping the vocal. |
| **Key** | input · sidechain | input | No control. Route a signal into the plugin's sidechain input in your host and the compressor follows it instead of its own input. **Threshold** and **SC HPF** apply to the key. See *Notes*. |
| **Iron** | off · on | on | The output transformer stage. Off is the compressor with no iron, which is what the reference hardware is on its own. |
| **Iron Flavor** | Punch · Weight · Clean | Clean | The same three voicings as Remanence. Clean is the one the reference chain uses. |
| **Iron Drive** | -12 to +12 dB | -6.0 | How hard the transformer is pushed. A color control, not a level control: the drive is level-compensated, so turning it up adds harmonics rather than volume. |
| **Mix** | 0 to 100% | 100 | Parallel blend. The dry path is the untouched input, so this is real parallel compression. The iron sits in the compressed path only. See *Notes*. |
| **Output** | -24 to +24 dB | 0.0 | Final trim, applied *after* the mix, so it works at any Mix setting, unless Auto Gain is on. |
| **Oversampling** | OFF · 2X · 4X · 8X | 4X | Only the `IRON` stage runs oversampled, because it is the only part that makes harmonics; the compressor itself does not. With Iron off it costs you nothing audible. |
| **Auto Gain** | off · on | off | Matches output loudness to input, so an A/B compares tone rather than level. Works at any Mix setting here. See *Controls every plugin shares*. |

title: Manual > Keelson > Readings
text:
GAIN REDUCTION
:   Gain reduction over time, newest at the right, with the current reduction
    printed above it. Beside it, a needle shows the same reduction the way a
    hardware meter would. The trace is for the shape, the needle for a glance.

KEY INT
:   The detector is following the plugin's own input.

KEY EXT
:   A lit dot and `KEY EXT`: the detector is following a sidechain. The key's
    level is drawn faintly behind the trace.

> **Watch the shape, not just the depth.** On AUTO the release is
> program-dependent, so the trace shows the compressor deciding how long to hold
> on: short dips for transients, long slopes for sustained passages. If the trace
> never returns toward zero between phrases, the threshold is too low or the
> release too slow for the material.

title: Manual > Keelson > Starting points
text:
**Mix glue.** 2:1, Attack 10, Release AUTO, Threshold set for 2 to 3 dB on the
loudest sections. Iron on, Clean. This is the setting the plugin exists for, and
it is the factory default.

**Drum bus.** 4:1, Attack 3 ms, Release 0.3 s, aiming for 4 to 6 dB. The faster
release brings the room up between hits. If the kick is doing all the work, reach
for SC HPF before Threshold.

**Heavy pump.** 10:1, Attack 0.1 ms, Release 0.1 s, well past 6 dB. Not subtle,
and not glue. This is the compressor as an effect.

**Hearing the iron.** The three presets under the **Iron** submenu load one
flavor each, with Iron Drive raised from its -6 dB default to 0. That is clearly
audible color on a hot bus. The compression stays at its defaults, so only the
transformer changes between them. Audition all three on the same section, then
back Iron Drive off to taste.

**Parallel.** Any of the above with Mix at 30 to 50%. Because the dry path is the
untouched input, you can compress far harder than you otherwise would and blend
it back underneath.

**If it sounds smaller rather than glued,** the attack is probably too fast. Go
to 10 or 30 ms before touching anything else.

title: Manual > Keelson > Notes > The idea
text:
A bus compressor is not a compressor you happen to put on the mix bus. It is a
different instrument. It is slow enough to let transients through and gentle
enough to be left on. It is useful mostly for what it does to the *relationship*
between things, not to any one of them. Two decibels of it across a mix does more
than ten decibels of anything else.

This is a VCA bus compressor of the classic kind: fixed ratios, switched attack
and release, and a program-dependent AUTO release. It has one addition, and that
addition is the reason it exists in this form.

**The output iron is part of the instrument.** The hardware this was voiced
against has no input or output transformers of its own. It is run here into a
pair of outboard passive transformer boxes. That pair is a target in its own
right, so it is modeled *as well as* the compressor alone, not instead of it. The
`IRON` stage is the same transformer model Remanence ships, switched to the same
three voicings. It can be turned off. "No iron" is what the compressor is by
itself, so that is a real setting, not a bypass.

title: Manual > Keelson > Notes > What AUTO does
text:
The AUTO release is not only a slower release. The circuit it comes from combines
**two** time constants. A small capacitor charges at once and lets short peaks go
quickly. A large capacitor charges only if compression carries on for a while.
After that, the slow constant takes over.

So the release time depends on *how long you have been compressing*, not on how
hard. A snare hit is let go fast. A loud chorus breathes out slowly. That is why
AUTO survives material that fixed release times pump on, and why most bus
compression is done on it. It is the default here.

The two constants come from the published component values of that circuit:
750k with 0.47 uF, and 91k with 6.8 uF. **How they blend is our model, not a
measurement**, and the beta notes say so. If it sounds wrong on your material,
that is useful information and worth sending back.

title: Manual > Keelson > Notes > The attack, and the parallel path
text:
The slow end of the Attack is the point. At 30 ms, transients pass through
untouched and only what follows is compressed. That is the difference between
glue and flattening. Fast attacks on a mix bus dull the front of everything.

Mix is a real parallel blend, not a wet/dry on a finished sound, because the dry
path is the untouched input. The iron sits in the compressed path only. When you
blend a compressor back against the source at a desk, the dry never went through
the compressor or its output transformer.

title: Manual > Keelson > Notes > The sidechain
text:
Route a signal into the plugin's sidechain input in your host. The compressor
follows that signal instead of its own input from the first moment it carries
signal. The display's header reads `KEY EXT` and draws the key's level behind
the gain reduction. With nothing routed, nothing changes. Threshold and SC HPF
apply to the key. A mono key into a stereo bus is the normal case.

Once a key has carried signal, the compressor stays on it until playback
restarts or you bypass and un-bypass the plugin. If you remove the source
mid-session, the compression stops. It does not go back to the input on its own.

title: Manual > Clew
text: A spring reverb, built from the physics of the coil rather than sampled.

title: Manual > Clew > Controls
text:
| Control | Range | Default | What it does |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Mode** | Mono · Stereo | Stereo | Topology, not width. Mono is one tank, with the input summed and the wet centered, as the hardware does it. Stereo is a tank per channel, slightly detuned from each other. Switching clears the tail. |
| **Decay** | 1.2 to 4.0 s | 2.0 | The damper: how long the springs ring. It is the same number at every frequency up to about 1 kHz, so the low end does not outlast the mids. The range spans the real tanks' short, medium and long grades. It changes only the loss; nothing else moves. |
| **Low Cut** | Off · 50 · 80 · 100 Hz | 50 | A high-pass *into* the tank, on the wet path only. Low end excites a spring into a boom that the tail then multiplies. The tank makers' own advice is a 50 to 100 Hz high-pass ahead of the driver. Off is a deliberate choice. |
| **Drive** | 0 to 100% | 0 | How hard the springs are driven into the input stage. Level-compensated, so it changes the sound rather than the volume. At 0 the stage is out of the circuit. With Limit off, this is the snarl of the vintage units. |
| **Limit** | off · on | off | A fixed, fast, program-dependent limiter ahead of the tank, stereo-linked. It is the professional studio spring's way of stopping transients from crashing the springs. On is the polite spring. Off with Drive up is the opposite personality. |
| **Mix** | 0 to 100% | 30 | Dry/wet. 100% is the wet tank alone, for a send. |
| **Output** | -24 to +24 dB | 0.0 | Trim after the blend. |
| **Auto Gain** | off · on | off | Matches output loudness to input, so an A/B compares tone rather than level. Tail-aware: it does not duck while the springs ring on after the input stops. See *Controls every plugin shares*. |

title: Manual > Clew > Controls
text:
One sentence about the low end. A spring's lowest frequencies travel the coil
most slowly, and on a bare model they would ring longest. Clew applies its loss
the way the tank's damper does, for each moment the signal spends in the spring.
So Decay is the same number from the bass to about 1 kHz, and a little shorter
above that, where the coil stops carrying signal. The low end still excites the
springs hardest, and every hardware spring product filters the input for that.
Low Cut is that filter. If the tail sounds boomy on a full mix, raise Low Cut
before reaching for Decay.

**On a mono track, pick the mono/stereo variant**: *(mono/stereo)* in Pro Tools,
*Mono→Stereo* in Logic. With Mode at Stereo, that feeds both tanks from the one
source, which is the "wide from mono" starting point below. The plain mono
variant runs one channel out and is only for a track that must stay mono.

title: Manual > Clew > Readings
text:
The display has two faces. **Click it to switch.** The plugin remembers which
you chose.

SPRING TANK - LIVE
:   The tank itself, seen from above with the lid off: the two springs between
    the drive end on the left and the pickup on the right. Each spring carries
    its own wave, drawn from what the engine is doing right now. A hit enters on
    the left, travels to the pickup, reflects and comes back, the shorter spring
    ahead of the longer one. When the transport stops or the plugin is bypassed,
    the springs settle. In Stereo the picture shows the left channel's tank.
    The springs move as a spring is seen to move: the slow motion, not the
    audio-rate wave. Light `SCOPE` in the display's header and they carry the raw
    wave instead, as an oscilloscope would show it. It is a display choice,
    remembered with the session; the sound is the same either way.

title: Manual > Clew > Readings
text:
WET TAIL - LIVE
:   Eight seconds of the wet signal the plugin is producing right now, scrolling
    right to left, with frequency on the vertical axis from 40 Hz to 6 kHz. It is
    not a picture of an impulse response. It is your own material going through
    the springs. The chirps show as short diagonal streaks and the drips as
    repeating columns. Turning Drive up puts new harmonics into the picture as
    it happens. In Stereo the left and right tanks are drawn in two tints, so you
    can see the two tanks disagree. The dashed line marks the frequency above
    which a torsional spring stops carrying signal, about 4 kHz on this tank.
    That is why a spring sounds the way it does, and why little appears above
    the line.

Stop the transport or engage bypass and the display scrolls to empty. It shows
what is happening, not what happened.

title: Manual > Clew > Starting points
text:
**On a guitar, amp-style.** Mono, Decay around 1.8 s, Low Cut 100 Hz, a touch
of Drive, Limit off, Mix 20 to 30%. That is the tank in the back of the combo.

**Surf.** Mono, Decay 2.8 s, Drive around 35%, Limit off, and run the Mix well
past where it seems sensible. The splash is the point.

**Dub send.** Mono, Decay near maximum, Drive 50%, Mix 100% on a send. Push the
send level rather than Drive when you want it to crash harder on a hit.

**The studio spring.** Stereo, Limit on, Low Cut 100 Hz, Decay 2.0 s, Drive 0.
Transients are caught before the springs are, so vocals and drums can go through
it without the boing.

**Two tanks, clean.** Stereo, Decay 2.4 s, Low Cut 80 Hz, no Drive, no Limit.
The budget stereo spring unit of the seventies: one tank per side and nothing in
the way.

**Wide from mono.** Any source, Stereo, everything else as it was. The two
detuned tanks decorrelate the tail, and a mono track comes back wider than it
went in, without a widener.

The first five are factory presets: *Amp Tank*, *Surf*, *Dub Tank*, *Pro Spring*
and *Two Tanks*.

title: Manual > Clew > Notes > The idea
text:
A spring reverb is a length of coiled wire with a magnet at each end. One magnet
twists the spring in time with the signal. The twist travels down the coil and
reflects off the far end, and the other magnet reads what comes back. What makes
it sound like a spring rather than a delay is that the coil is *dispersive*: the
twist does not travel at one speed. Low frequencies arrive first and the highs
straggle in behind them, so every reflection is smeared into a short upward
chirp. That chirp is the drip, the splash, the sound you hear when a tank is
kicked.

This is not a recording of a spring. It solves that propagation directly: the
dispersive round trip, the alternating sign of each reflection, the scattering
at the joint in the middle of each spring that fills the patter between the big
drips, and the loss along the way. The tank it solves is the long two-spring tank
that lives inside most guitar amplifiers. That gives it the hardware's honesty in
two places. **Decay** is the damper on the tank. It changes only how much is lost
for each moment the signal spends in the spring. The spacing of the drips and
the shape of the chirp never move with it, as on the real thing. **Stereo** is
not a width control. It runs two separate tanks, one per
channel, detuned from each other by about as much as two units off the same
production line differ. That keeps a stereo image intact and widens a mono source
for free.

title: Manual > Clew > Notes > The idea
text:
The name is the old word for a ball of thread: the one paid out behind you into
the labyrinth so you can find your way back, which is where *clue* comes from. A
coil of wire that sends a signal out and returns it seemed close enough.

title: Manual > Undercroft
text: A room reverb. You set the room's dimensions and what each surface is made of, and it works out the rest.

title: Manual > Undercroft > Controls
text:
| Control | Range | Default | What it does |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Length** | 2 to 30 m | 7.0 | The long dimension of the room. |
| **Width** | 2 to 20 m | 5.2 | The short one. |
| **Height** | 2 to 12 m | 3.4 | The ceiling's mean height; it slopes along the length. |
| **Distance** | 0.5 to 25 m | 4.0 | Speakers to listener. Further away means later and quieter first reflections and more of the late field. If you ask for more than the room allows, the display says `ROOM LIMIT`, the readout gives the most that fits (`5.1 m max`), and the plugin uses that. |
| **Floor**, **Ceiling**, **Walls** | one material each | hardwood, drywall, stone | What each surface is made of, from the table in *Notes*. Click the right half of a surface's stepper to move one row toward the reflective end, and the left half to move back (shift-click and right-click also step back). Off leaves a surface out entirely: an open ceiling is a courtyard. |
| **Link Walls** | on · off | on | On: one material for all four walls. Off: each wall has its own stepper. |
| **Contents** | Empty · Sparse · Furnished · Full | Empty | What is in the room. No material table describes furniture, but a measured room absorbs more than its bare surfaces say, so this covers 0, 25, 50 or 100% of the floor with the absorber row. |
| **Mode** | Mono · Stereo | Stereo | Mono sums the input to one speaker in the room and listens with one ear. Stereo puts the left and right channels on two speakers **Speakers** apart and listens with a pair of ears **Ears** apart, so every reflection arrives at each ear at its own time and level. |
| **Speakers** | 1.2 · 2.4 · 3.6 m | 1.2 m | Stereo only; dimmed in Mono. How far apart the two speakers stand. Wider excites the room from two more different places, so the left and right reflections differ more. If the room cannot hold the pair, it is moved sideways first, then narrowed, and the display says which. |
| **Ears** | 20 · 40 · 80 · 160 cm | 20 cm | Stereo only; dimmed in Mono. 20 cm is a head; 160 cm is a spaced microphone pair. Wider hears every reflection, and the tail, with more difference between the two sides: a wider, less correlated wet and a weaker mono fold. At 20 cm the low end of the tail is nearly mono, as it is to a listener. |
| **Pre-Delay** | 0 to 200 ms | 0 | A delay line in front of the room. Not a room fact: a real room's pre-delay is the first-reflection time, which the display shows. But every reverb has one, and it is labeled as what it is. |
| **Low Cut** | Off · 80 · 160 · 250 Hz | Off | A high-pass on the send, in front of the room, in the same category as Pre-Delay. The room itself does what its surfaces say; a stone room rightly rings for seconds at 125 to 250 Hz. This is the filter every reverb send carries to keep that out of the mix. Not level-compensated: cutting makes the tail lighter, never louder. It sits where a room's excess lives, higher than Clew's spring corners. |
| **Mix** | 0 to 100% | 30 | Dry/wet. The wet is the reflections and the late field only, never the direct sound. The dry is the direct sound. |
| **Output** | -24 to +24 dB | 0.0 | Trim after the blend. |
| **Auto Gain** | off · on | off | Matches output loudness to input, so an A/B compares tone rather than level. Tail-aware: it does not duck while the room rings on after the input stops. See *Controls every plugin shares*. |

title: Manual > Undercroft > Controls
text:
There is no oversampling control and no latency. The engine is linear, and the
room's delays are the only delays.

title: Manual > Undercroft > Readings
text:
ROOM
:   A model of what you built, drawn to scale: the angled plan and its sloping
    ceiling, each surface shaded and named by its material, a surface that is Off
    drawn dashed, a one-meter grid on the floor, and the speakers and ears
    standing in it. Drag to turn it. Double-click to return to the starting view.
    The view is saved with the session. While audio runs, the early reflections
    light up in the room. Each first reflection is drawn as its whole path from
    speaker to surface to ear. Each second reflection is drawn as the point where
    it strikes. A path lights only while that reflection's energy is rising, so a
    transient lights the surfaces it reaches in the order it reaches them, and
    the light fades in about a third of a second. Silence and a sustained note
    both leave the room unlit. Third bounces are not drawn. They double the count
    and say nothing the second bounce did not.

VOLUME
:   The room's volume, in cubic meters and cubic feet. The first of the figures
    along the foot of the screen, on two lines.

FIRST REFLECTION
:   When the earliest bounce arrives after the direct sound. This is what a real
    room's pre-delay is.

TAIL FROM
:   Where the countable reflections hand over to the late field.

CPU
:   At the end of that line, while audio is running: the share of one core the
    engine is using. It is there because Stereo costs several times Mono, four
    sets of reflections against one, and nothing else on the panel would tell
    you.

title: Manual > Undercroft > Readings
text:
PREDICTED / MEASURED
:   The second line prints the decay time, `T60`, as pairs in three bands: `LOW`
    is 125 to 250 Hz, `MID` is 500 Hz to 2 kHz, `HIGH` is 4 to 8 kHz. T60 is the
    time a sound takes to fall by 60 dB after it stops. **Predicted** is the decay
    the room's geometry and materials imply: an estimate from the surfaces, the
    way an acoustician predicts a room before it is built. In the low band the
    prediction is the decay of the room's own resonances (see *Below the
    Schroeder frequency*), which is often longer than the textbook figure.
    **Measured** is the plugin's own answer. It renders an impulse through the
    room it just built and reads the decay off that, band by band. The pairs let
    you see where they disagree. A room with one absorptive wall among
    reflective ones decays differently from what the averaged prediction says,
    and the measured figure is the one you are hearing.

PREDICTED / MEASURING
:   What the second line reads while a new room is being solved.

Change a dimension or a surface while audio is running and the old room fades
into the new one over about 80 ms, keeping the tail. Nothing drops out.

title: Manual > Undercroft > Starting points
text:
**Small room.** 4.5 x 3.6 x 2.6 m, hardwood floor, drywall everywhere else,
2 m away. A bedroom with the furniture out. Put a vocal in it at Mix 20% for a
sense of place rather than a reverb.

**Stone hall.** 16 x 9 x 7 m, stone on every surface, 9 m away. Long, bright and
honest about it. This is what a stone room does, not a plate pretending to be one.

**Courtyard.** 10 x 7 x 4 m, concrete floor, stone walls, and the ceiling Off.
Reflections from four walls and the ground, and nothing from above. The open
ceiling lets the sound out, so the room decays far faster than its stone walls
alone would suggest. Both figures account for it.

**Dead room.** 6 x 4.5 x 2.8 m, hardwood floor, absorber on every other surface.
The early reflections of a treated room with almost no tail. Try it on drums at
Mix 40% before reaching for a compressor.

**Adobe room.** 9 x 7 x 4.5 m, hardwood floor, plywood ceiling, adobe walls.
The unmeasured row, in a room like the ones it will be measured in.

**Tiled room.** 3 x 2.4 x 2.5 m, tiles everywhere but a drywall ceiling. A
bathroom, 1.5 m from the singer.

**Live room.** 9 x 6.5 x 4 m, hardwood floor, drywall, and diffusers on two
opposite walls with Link Walls off. A tracking room that was built to be one.

**Studio Two.** 18.3 x 11.7 x 7.3 m, parquet over concrete, an absorbent
ceiling, paneled walls with the far end diffusing, and the floor Full of
screens and instruments. The dimensions are the published ones. The listener is
9 m out, the mid-room position of the famous photographs.

All eight are factory presets.

title: Manual > Undercroft > Notes > The idea
text:
Every reverb so far in this manual has been an object: a plate, a spring. This
one is a room, and the only things you set are the room. Give it a length, a
width and a height. Say what each surface is made of. Put the speakers and the
listener some distance apart. It works out what that room does to a sound. There
is no decay knob, because the decay is a consequence of the walls. There is no
"size" knob, because the size is the size.

It does this in two stages, as a real room does. The **early reflections** are
solved exactly. Each is a real path from the speakers to a wall, floor or ceiling
and on to the listener, up to three bounces deep, with that surface's absorption
applied on every bounce. The **late field** is the wash after the first few dozen
reflections have merged. It is a dense network whose decay in each frequency band
is set from the room's volume, its surface area, and what those surfaces absorb.
The two are joined at the point where a room's own reflections stop being
countable. For these rooms that is about two mean free paths in, where the mean
free path is the average distance a sound travels between one bounce and the
next.

The materials are not adjectives. Each surface is a row from a published table of
measured absorption, band by band. The material is named the way the table
names it: not "wood" but a hardwood floor laid over concrete, not "soft" but 50
mm of rockwool. That is why a stone hall and a tiled bathroom behave differently
in the low band and the high band, rather than only being "long" and "bright".

title: Manual > Undercroft > Notes > The idea
text:
The room's shape is deliberately not a box. The plan is a trapezoid with no two
walls parallel, and the ceiling slopes along the length, so no two surfaces face
each other squarely. That is how a good room is built, and it is why the early
reflections do not flutter. The shape is not a control, but it is not decoration
either. The room's low resonances are those of this shape, so it is heard. See
*Below the Schroeder frequency*.

An undercroft is the vaulted room beneath a building. It seemed the right name
for a reverb that is a space you go down into.

title: Manual > Undercroft > Notes > The materials
text:
Each row is a measured, random-incidence absorption curve from the annex of
Vorländer's *Auralization* (2nd ed., 2020), which draws on the PTB round-robin
database. The steppers run from the most absorptive surface to the most
reflective, so every click to the right adds room.

title: Manual > Undercroft > Notes > The materials
text:
| Row | What it is |
|:--|:--|
| **Off** | The surface is left out of the room. It still bounds the volume, but nothing reflects from it. |
| **Absorber** | Rockwool, 50 mm, 80 kg/m3. |
| **Curtain** | Studio curtains hung 22 cm off the wall. |
| **Carpet** | 9 mm tufted pile carpet on felt underlay. |
| **Plywood** | Thin plywood paneling, which absorbs the low band and reflects the rest. |
| **Drywall** | Two layers of 13 mm plasterboard on a steel frame with 50 mm of wool behind it. |
| **Diffuser** | A quadratic-residue diffuser panel over plasterboard. The absorption is the plasterboard's. The panel scatters what it reflects, so this wall stops producing a hard first reflection and feeds the late field instead. |
| **Hardwood** | A hardwood floor, two layers, 33 mm on sleepers over concrete: the modern floor over a slab, not the old suspended floor on joists. |
| **Brick** | Brick wall, stuccoed with a rough finish. |
| **Stone** | Limestone wall. |
| **Glass** | A single 3 mm pane. It absorbs a little low end by flexing and reflects everything else. |
| **Adobe** | Unmeasured. No published table has an earth wall, so this row is the annex's average for hard rendered surfaces, and the panel says so. It will be replaced by a measurement when one exists. |
| **Concrete** | Smooth, unpainted concrete. |
| **Tiles** | Ceramic tiles with a smooth surface, the same numbers as marble. |

title: Manual > Undercroft > Notes > Below the Schroeder frequency
text:
Every room has a frequency below which it stops behaving like reflections and
starts behaving like resonances: standing waves between the walls. That
crossover is the Schroeder frequency, and it sits between about 40 and 250 Hz
for rooms this size. Below it, this engine models the room's own modes. A mode is
one standing wave across the room's length, width or height. Each mode decays by
the walls it runs between. A wave along the length grazes the floor and ceiling
and barely feels them, which is why the bass of a room outlives its mid-range.
Each mode is heard at each ear from where that ear stands in the wave. Above the
crossover, the reflections and the diffuse tail take over, and the join is
seamless.

So what you hear down there is the boom of a particular room, not a smooth
decay. A bass note that sits on a mode rings longer than its neighbor, as it does
in a real room. A spaced pair of Ears hears the two sides of a wave differently.
At the default 20 cm, both ears hear the bass as one signal, as a head does. The
predicted `T60` in the low band is the decay those modes imply, which is usually
longer than the textbook diffuse figure would say. The measured one is the engine
agreeing with it.

The non-parallel shape is still not a control, but its benefit is in the model.
The modes are those of the room as drawn, so a pair of resonances that a
rectangular room would stack on one frequency are split apart here, as a
well-built room splits them. Above the crossover, the shape does what you would
expect: it keeps the early reflections from repeating.

title: Manual > Feedback
text:
Bugs, crashes, CPU problems, and above all anything that sounds wrong:

**support@fruitlessresearch.com**

**Please quote the version and build date when you report anything.** Click the
**FR mark** at the top left of any panel; both are on the line under the plugin's
name. They are the only thing that ties a report to one specific binary.

title: Changelog > 1.0.0 > Changed — the release week (2026-08-12 → 2026-08-19)
text:
**The first public release.** Everything below has accumulated since the 0.4.0 beta of
2026-08-08; the jump from 0.4.0 to 1.0.0 is the end of the beta programme, not a batch of new
features. There will be no further beta before release — this is it.

What changes for you beyond the entries below:

- **The plugins are no longer time-limited builds.** No 45-day window, no expiry counting down
  in the title band. Each plugin instead runs complete for 14 days from the first time you open
  its window, and a license removes the limit permanently. See *Changed* immediately below.
- **The title band is quiet.** It carried `v0.4.0 BETA - BUILT 09 AUG 2026`; a licensed plugin
  now shows just its name. Version, build date and license status moved into the panel behind
  the **FR mark**, which is what to quote in a bug report.
- **Downloads are named for the version alone** — `FruitlessResearch-1.0.0-macos.pkg`. The build
  date came out of release filenames, because the two reasons it was there were both beta
  reasons: frequent rebuilds at one version, and a beta clock that restarted per build.
- **The manual drops its beta chapter** and gains a section on the demo and licensing. Every
  panel figure in it was recaptured against this release.

Everything here landed between the entry below being written and 1.0.0 actually shipping.

title: Changelog > 1.0.0 > Changed — the release week (2026-08-12 → 2026-08-19)
text:
- **Every gain-type knob now glides.** Drive, trim and makeup were applied as one constant per
  audio block, which clicked and zippered on low sustained tones when moved or automated. They
  now smooth per-sample the way Mix always has, across the whole line.
- **Trammel and Keelson: SC HPF tops out at 185 Hz, not 400.** Beta-reported: at high corners
  the compressor's gain crept back up on program material. 185 Hz is the traditional top of the
  SSL-style sidechain mod this control descends from; existing sessions above 185 recall at 185.
- **Amnesia: FEEDBACK is now an audio taper.** The oscillation region lived in the top ~8% of
  the knob; it now occupies the top quarter, with the usable echo range spread over the rest.
  Saved sessions and presets are remapped so the sound you had is the sound you keep.
- **Amnesia: a tempo rail replaces the bare delay knob's relationship to the host.** Host sync,
  subdivision cells (with dotted/triplet), and **NUDGE** — a push/pull percentage around the
  grid that survives tempo changes, because a proportion does where milliseconds cannot.
- **New factory presets across five plugins.** Amnesia gains the missing *Slapback*;
  Fifty-Fifty completes its alignment grid with *7.5 ips IEC*; Jointer gains *Drum Bus Shave*
  (the clipper as a sound, not a delivery spec); Keelson gains an *Iron* submenu that
  auditions each transformer flavour with the compression held at defaults. Plus the
  **TW Walsh signature series** — session-saved artist presets under a *TW Walsh* submenu in
  Amnesia, Firmament, Remanence, Trammel and Jointer.
- **The FR-mark popover now names the exact build**: `v1.0.0 (384de9dbf)` — version plus the
  commit that built the binary. Quote it in reports; it is the one identifier that cannot be
  stale two different ways like a date can.
- **Windows installs from a signed installer** — VST3 *and* AAX, with per-format checkboxes and
  an entry in Add/Remove Programs — instead of an unzip-and-copy. **Pro Tools on Windows is
  now supported.**
- **Feedback goes to support@fruitlessresearch.com** (the manual's Feedback page; the personal
  address in beta manuals is retired).

title: Changelog > 1.0.0 > Changed — one license-gated binary; demo windows replace beta builds (2026-08-11)
text:
The line now ships a single build of each plugin, gated by license — there are no separate
beta and public builds any more. What you'll see:

- **Unlicensed = a free 14-day demo, per plugin, full processing.** The window starts the
  first time you *open that plugin's editor* — installing, scanning, or loading a session
  does not start it. A DEMO badge next to the plugin name counts the days.
- **When the demo ends, the plugin steps aside instead of breaking your session**: audio
  passes through unprocessed, with a brief (~1 s) faded silence every ~45 s so an unpaid
  bounce can't masquerade as a finished master. Never within the first 30 s, never more
  than ~1 s at a time — looping or stopping the transport can't make it worse. A bar on
  the panel says exactly what's happening and what to do.
- **Licensing is paste-and-go**: click the FR mark, paste your license, reload the session.
  A licensed plugin is clean forever — no clock, no server, no account.
- **Existing 0.4.0 beta builds are unaffected** — they keep their compiled-in window
  (to ~23 Sep 2026) and ignore licenses entirely. The license system arrives with the next
  build you receive; testers will get licenses alongside it.

title: Changelog > 1.0.0 > 🔴 Fixed — review pass, second batch (2026-08-09)
text:
- **Delay compensation is now correct from the moment a session opens.** Plugins used to tell
  the host their latency only once audio started flowing, so hosts that lock compensation in
  at plugin-load ran the first moments — or in some hosts the whole session — misaligned.
- **The OUTPUT meters no longer miss peaks between frames.** They previously sampled roughly
  one block in three at typical buffer sizes, so short transients could peak without the
  needle showing it. Every block's peak now reaches the meter (the gain-reduction meters got
  this fix earlier).
- **Fifty-Fifty's TAPE RESPONSE panel no longer briefly shows a flat line at plugin open.**
  Before the first real measurement landed it drew a fabricated dead-flat curve; it now draws
  nothing until it has measured something.
- **Saving a preset to a full disk or read-only folder no longer pretends it worked.** The
  preset bar used to display the new name as current while no file existed.
- **Amnesia's tap tempo now records into automation properly** in touch/latch modes.
- **Lower CPU with editors open**: the two busiest panels (Firmament, Jointer) redraw only
  their live displays instead of the whole window 20× a second, settled meters stop
  repainting, and Jointer's limiter stage costs roughly half what it did at high sample rates.
- Internal hardening you shouldn't hear, listed for completeness: guards against empty audio
  buffers from the host, a NaN entering a compressor sidechain no longer silently disables
  compression, expired-beta builds zero their meters ("fail-open must look open"), and the
  three engine-style plugins now share one prepare/process scaffold so this class of drift
  can't recur.

title: Changelog > 1.0.0 > 🔴 Fixed — a full-line review pass (2026-08-09)
text:
- **Fifty-Fifty: the tape's drive no longer changes with the OVERSAMPLING setting.** At
  oversampling Off (and, less so, 2x) the record-side EQ drove the tape up to ~9 dB hotter than
  intended, so the same knob positions saturated far harder than at 4x/8x. The frequency
  response was unaffected — only the amount of saturation — which is why it survived every
  response check. If you had dialled a sound at OS Off, expect it cleaner now; the 4x default
  (and 8x) are unchanged.
- **Fifty-Fifty now reports its true latency.** The wow/flutter stage always delayed the signal
  by ~4 samples (≈0.1 ms) without telling the host, so a parallel duplicate of a processed track
  combed slightly. Delay compensation now accounts for it.
- **Firmament no longer fades in at the start of a render.** A freshly loaded instance ramped
  its output and mix up from silence over the first 20 ms, so a bounce from the top of the
  session started with a fade-in. It now starts at the dialled values from the first sample.
- **Firmament and Jointer: starting bypassed now means bypassed from sample zero.** A session
  saved with BYPASS engaged briefly crossfaded the processed signal out at the start of playback
  instead of being clean-dry immediately. The other five plugins already did this correctly.
- **Firmament: turning DECAY can no longer (rarely) cut the reverb tail dead.** A thread race
  could promote a decay-only change to a full rebuild, which resets the ringing plate.
- **Amnesia: repeats no longer start early and pitch-bent after opening a session.** Every
  session open (or buffer-size change) restarted the delay line short and slewed it up to the
  dialled time over ~150 ms — audible as bent first repeats at the head of a render.
- **Amnesia: track freeze and tail bounces no longer truncate the echo train.** The plugin told
  hosts its tail was a flat 2 seconds regardless of delay time or feedback; it now reports an
  honest estimate (up to 30 s near self-oscillation).
- **Presets: recalling a user preset now always produces the same sound.** Parameters added to
  a plugin after a preset was saved kept whatever you had dialled since, instead of returning to
  their defaults — the same preset could recall differently depending on what you did before.
- **Fixed a crash-on-close**: closing the plugin window while its preset save dialog (or preset
  menu) was open could crash the host.

title: Changelog > 1.0.0 > 🔴 Fixed — the Pro Tools window now follows GUI SIZE
text:
- **In Pro Tools, changing GUI SIZE resized the panel and not the window**, so anything above 100%
  drew the panel larger than the window containing it and clipped the right-hand column. Reported
  from a real session on 2026-08-08. **Correct in Logic and Live all along**, and wrong in Pro Tools
  at every step except 100% — so it arrived with AAX rather than being caused by it.
- The cause was one component doing two jobs. GUI SIZE was applied as a *transform*, which changes
  how a panel is drawn but not what it reports as its size. Every host that composes the transform
  read the right number; AAX asks the plugin for its bounds directly and read the base size forever.
  The panel and the window it lives in are now two separate components, so the size a host reads is
  the size the panel is actually drawn at.
- ⚠️ **Nothing about the panels themselves changed** — same layout, same fixed pixel geometry, same
  five sizes, same corner and right-click menu. If you use AU or VST3 you will not be able to tell
  this release from the last one.

title: Changelog > 1.0.1 > Fixed
text:
A defect release. Nothing new on any panel, no parameter or preset changes — sessions saved
under 1.0.0 recall identically. Four things found in real sessions (three of them by TW, one
by a measurement written for a different plugin) are fixed; everything else is 1.0.0's bytes
rebuilt. The FR-mark popover reads `v1.0.1 (<commit>)`.

title: Changelog > 1.0.1 > Fixed
text:
- **Firmament: a loud distortion burst when inserted on a track that was already playing.**
  A freshly inserted instance ran its first ~50 ms of wet signal ~90 dB too hot — a clipped
  blast — because the wet make-up was primed before the plate calibration that sets it had
  been computed. Inserting while stopped never showed it (the window flushes through
  silence), which is why it survived every stopped-load session and both validators; it only
  ever happened on the first buffer of a fresh instance. Fixed by priming after the
  calibration; verified insert-while-playing in Live.
- **Jointer: the knee was applied twice, and COMPENSATE overshot.** After the Mix blend the
  clipper re-ran its knee curve "to guarantee the ceiling", which kneed every sample the first
  pass had already placed inside the knee. A peak driven to the ceiling came out
  0.4 / 0.7 / 1.2 / 1.6 dB lower than the manual's table at Knee 3 / 6 / 12 / 24, and with
  COMPENSATE on the knee's local gain was 1.77× instead of the designed 4/3 — the "+2.5 dB"
  was nearly +5. The second pass is now a hard bound at the ceiling, which does nothing to a
  signal the first pass already shaped. **What you will hear:** at the same settings Jointer
  now lands up to 1.6 dB closer to the ceiling with COMPENSATE off, and COMPENSATE is gentler
  than it was. The manual's Compensate tables were always the design figures; the plugin now
  matches them.
- **Jointer: CLIP TRACE drew a red CLIPPED band while BYPASSED.** The scope kept pushing
  Drive-scaled peaks against an untouched signal, so it showed clipping exactly Drive dB
  tall on audio the plugin was not touching. Bypassed, the trace now shows the envelope with
  no red and dims like every other measured display; KNEE SHAPE and Firmament's decay curve
  dim under BYPASS too.
- **Remanence, Keelson (IRON) and Fifty-Fifty (colour mode): the bottom octave drifted at 8×
  oversampling and above.** The transformer stage's low-frequency pre/de-emphasis pair no
  longer cancelled at 384 kHz (−0.4 dB below 50 Hz) or 768 kHz (−0.9 dB), sign per flavour.
  The pair now runs in double precision and cancels to 0.00 dB at every rate; the harmonic
  profile is unchanged. At 2× and 4× the drift was ≤0.1 dB, so most sessions will not hear a
  difference.

title: Changelog > 1.1.0 > New
text:
A new plugin, and it is free. Nothing changes for the seven you may already have — no
parameter, preset or sound changes; sessions saved under 1.0.1 recall identically.

- **Clew — a spring reverb, free.** Built from the physics of the coil rather than from a
  recording: the dispersive round trip along a long two-spring tank, with the hardware's own
  honesty — DECAY is the damper and changes only the loss per trip, so the drips and the chirp
  never move with it. MONO is one honest tank; STEREO is two tanks detuned like two units off
  the same production line, which keeps an image and widens a mono source. A pre-tank LIMIT
  gives the studio-spring posture; DRIVE with LIMIT off gives the snarl. LOW CUT is the tank
  makers' own rumble filter into the springs, on by default at 50 Hz. The panel shows a live
  time-frequency view of the wet tail on your own material. Ten factory presets, from *Amp
  Tank* to *Dub Tank*. Get your license from the plugin's page — it goes through the same
  checkout at $0 and arrives by the same email — and it is also included with every purchase.

title: Changelog > 1.1.0 > Changed
text:
- **The license email and the manual now explain the attached license files** — one
  `.frlicense` per plugin, and the folder to put them in on macOS and Windows — as the
  alternative to pasting. Both folders are hidden by default, so both texts tell you to type
  the path rather than look for it.

title: Changelog > 1.2.0 > New
text:
A new paid plugin, and the reverbs learn to sit on a mono track. Nothing changes in what
the eight you may already have render: every fix below that touches a saved session says so
and keeps the session's sound.

title: Changelog > 1.2.0 > New
text:
- **Undercroft — a room you build. $59.** Set the room's length, width and height, choose a
  material for the floor, the ceiling and each wall from a table of published absorption
  measurements (hardwood, drywall, stone, tiles, plywood, absorber, diffuser, adobe…), leave a
  ceiling **Off** for a courtyard, put the speakers and the listener some metres apart, and
  the plugin works out what that room does to a sound: the early reflections by tracing the
  images of the source in each wall, and a late field whose delays and per-band losses come
  from the same geometry and the same table. **Mode** is Mono (one speaker, one ear) or Stereo
  (a pair 1.2 m apart heard by two ears 20 cm apart, so every reflection reaches each ear at
  its own time and level). **Contents** covers part of the floor with the absorber row for a
  furnished room. **Low Cut** is a high-pass on the send (Off / 80 / 160 / 250 Hz) for what a
  stone room rightly does at 125–250 Hz. The panel draws the room, lights each surface as a
  reflection passes through it, and prints the volume, the first-reflection time, where the
  tail begins, the decay time the geometry **predicts** in three bands and, beside it, the
  decay time the plugin **measures** from its own impulse response — and the CPU it is
  costing you while audio runs. Eight factory presets, from a bedroom to Studio Two. Joins the
  bundle, which becomes $359 for all eight paid plugins.

title: Changelog > 1.2.0 > Added
text:
- **Firmament: DRIVE is back, and it is the amplifier this time.** A fifth knob, between PRE-DELAY
  and DECAY: the V54 drive amplifier's tube stage pushed past the alignment EMT specified the plate
  at, into the plate. Level-compensated, so it changes the sound and not the volume; COMPRESS still
  does its hardware job of holding the amp in its clean range, so the two interact. **0 is the
  machine as specified**, with the stage out of the circuit — every saved session and every
  factory preset loads there and renders as before. One thing to know: the wet now arrives 6
  samples later than it did (0.13 ms at 48 kHz), at every DRIVE setting, because the stage's
  oversampler stays in the path so the timing cannot step when you touch the knob. The dry is
  untouched and nothing is reported to the host. (The first DRIVE, removed before 1.0, only scaled
  the wet — the plate itself is a sub-1 % THD device and stays one.)

title: Changelog > 1.2.0 > Added
text:
- **Firmament and Clew go on a mono track and come out stereo.** Both now offer a mono-in /
  stereo-out configuration: Pro Tools lists it as **(mono/stereo)** and switches the track to a
  stereo path from that insert on, Logic lists it as **Mono→Stereo**. Until now a mono track was
  offered only the mono variant, so the plate's two pickups and the spring's two tanks were summed
  to one channel — the "stuck in mono" that two Gearspace listeners reported, and rightly. On a
  stereo track nothing changes. The existing mono and stereo variants keep their identities, so
  saved sessions load as before. (Cubase runs a mono track's plugins in mono regardless; use a
  stereo FX channel there, as before.) Undercroft, still in the lab, has it too.

- **Trammel: a 2:1 ratio and a SLOW attack switch** — the two things the 1176AE added to the
  1176, suggested by God City. SLOW is a fixed 12 ms attack, the value of God City's own modded
  units (the AE's switch is 10 ms); while it is lit the ATTACK knob is out of the circuit and
  dimmed. Both load as they were in saved sessions and presets.
  ⚠️ One exception, stated plainly: a Pro Tools or VST3 **automation lane on Ratio** drawn at
  **20:1** before this version now plays ALL, because those hosts store a button choice as a
  fraction of the button count and there are now six. Redraw that lane. Lanes at 4:1, 8:1 and
  12:1, AU lanes, and everything that is not a Ratio lane are unaffected (measured, not
  reasoned: `trammel.state` asserts each of the four).

title: Changelog > 1.2.0 > Changed
text:
- **The output meters draw a larger arc.** Every plugin with the needle meter (Trammel,
  Remanence, Amnesia, Fifty-Fifty, Clew, Undercroft) sizes the arc to the height of its box
  rather than to a fixed fraction of its width, so the meter fills the space it is given. The
  reading, the scale and the colours are unchanged.
- **After checkout the page says so, and a lost license can be re-sent.** The buy button turns
  into "Done. Your license is on its way to <address>" when the overlay closes, and every plugin
  page and the downloads page carry a *lost your license?* form that re-sends every license an
  address holds. (Found from the Clew claims: one in fifteen people claimed twice because
  nothing on the page changed and the email had gone to spam.)

title: Changelog > 1.2.0 > Fixed
text:
- **Firmament: LOW CUT gets a MAKEUP option, and cuts by default.** Since 1.0.0 each LOW CUT
  position carried its own level compensation, solved so a pink-noise source would stay at the same
  level through the switch — up to 12 dB of makeup that a snare, a guitar or a voice, with far less
  low end than pink, never lost to the cut. Measured: +2 dB across the switch on pink noise, +6 dB
  on material from 50 Hz up. The compensation is now the **MAKEUP** LED beside LOW CUT: on, the
  reverb holds its level through the switch on bass-heavy material; off, the switch simply cuts,
  like the one on the EMT's drive amplifier, and can never make the reverb louder. New instances
  start with it off. **Sessions saved before this version load with MAKEUP on** and render exactly
  as they did the day they were saved; a session at the default LOW CUT (−4) sounds identical
  either way.

title: Changelog > 1.2.0 > Fixed
text:
- **Our plugin files are now named `<Plugin>_FR` on disk** (`Remanence_FR.vst3`,
  `Trammel_FR.component`, …), so they can no longer land on another maker's plugin of the same
  name. A user who owned Stillwell Audio's *Remanence* found ours had overwritten it: both
  installers wrote a bundle at the same path. The name you see in your DAW is unchanged, and so
  is everything a session or preset stores, because hosts identify a plugin by its code, not
  its file. **Upgrading:** the installer removes our old-named files first, so you do not end up
  with two of each. If you installed by dragging files in by hand (a beta zip, the manual
  install notes), delete the old `<Plugin>.vst3` / `.component` / `.aaxplugin` yourself, or your
  DAW may list each plugin twice.
- **Any single plugin can be left out of an install, on both platforms,** without wading through
  a grid of boxes. On both, tick "Choose individual plugins" and a list of the plugins opens up;
  leave it alone and every plugin in each chosen format is installed. A plugin whose
  destination already holds a bundle that is not ours starts unticked, with the reason shown.
  (Windows still has one uninstaller for the whole set; leaving a plugin out at install is the
  way to not have it.)
- **Changing the oversampling setting while audio is running no longer clicks** — Trammel,
  Remanence, Amnesia, Fifty-Fifty, Jointer and Keelson, which share the oversampling engine.
  Reported on Trammel. The incoming oversampler started from silence and ramped up over a few
  samples, and the plugin's reported latency stepped with the setting, which some hosts answer
  with a dropout of their own. The engine now keeps its filters primed across a change and
  reports one latency at every setting (the highest factor's, up to 6 samples at 48 kHz), so
  neither happens. Sessions recall identically; the only audible difference is the absence of
  the click.
- **Keelson's IRON button and Fifty-Fifty's oversampling setting no longer change the reported
  latency.** Keelson reported the oversampler's delay only while the iron was on, so switching it
  was a latency change to the host; the delay is now carried either way (six samples at 48 kHz)
  and the button is silent. Fifty-Fifty's tape centre tap is defined so that it is the same
  number of samples at every oversampling setting.

title: Changelog > 1.2.1 > Fixed
text:
A display release for Undercroft, the day after it shipped. Nothing changes in the sound of any
plugin, no parameter moved, and sessions saved under 1.2.0 recall identically.

- **Undercroft draws the room to scale.** The wire drawing was stretched across its box, so every
  height read at about a third of its true size against the length and width — a 3.4 m ceiling in a
  7 m room looked like a sixth of it instead of a half. It is now drawn with one scale in every
  direction, and it is larger: the room has the whole left of the display to itself.

title: Changelog > 1.2.1 > Changed
text:
- **Undercroft's output meter is replaced by its readings.** The right of the display now shows the
  room's volume, the first-reflection time, where the tail begins and the CPU cost, then the decay
  time in three bands as a small table: what the room's geometry predicts, and beneath it what the
  plugin measures from its own impulse response, in larger type than before. A level meter says
  little about a reverb's output; the decay figures are what change the next setting you reach for.

title: Changelog > 2.0.0 > New
text:
Every plugin gets a face of its own, and four of them a new sound. Each plugin now opens in a look
made for it, and one menu item puts the whole line back to the panel you know; a look changes
nothing you hear and is not stored in your session. Clew has a new spring engine and Undercroft a
new low end, and both change how sessions saved under 1.2.1 sound — each entry below says so.
Everything else recalls exactly as it was.

title: Changelog > 2.0.0 > New
text:
- **A look per plugin, and Classic.** Right-click the panel background: under **LOOK** is the
  plugin's own look (Van Nuys on Trammel, New York on Remanence, Osaka on Amnesia and Clew, Tokyo on
  Fifty-Fifty, Van Nuys olive on Jointer, Lahr on Firmament, Oxfordshire on Keelson, Lastingham on
  Undercroft) or **Classic**, the 1.2 panel. The choice is line-wide and remembered, like the GUI
  size. Two panels draw a control differently in their own look: Firmament's Decay is the plate's
  damping wheel, and Fifty-Fifty's output arc is a turning tape reel. Under Classic both are the knob
  and the arc they were.
- **Clew 2.0: a new spring engine.** Decay now means the same thing at every frequency up to about
  1 kHz: the low end no longer outlasts the mids, and the number on the knob is the decay you hear
  (it ran long before, by about a quarter at the short end). Each spring now scatters at its middle
  as a real coil does, so the patter between the big drips is denser, and the tank has its
  characteristic boing. **Every session saved under 1.2.1 sounds different** — the same tank, voiced
  closer to the real thing. If an old mix depended on the long low tail, try Low Cut Off and a longer
  Decay.
- **Undercroft's bass is the room's own.** Below the room's Schroeder frequency the tail is now its
  resonant modes, each decaying by the surfaces it runs along and heard where each ear stands, joined
  to the diffuse tail above. Bass tails ring longer and less evenly, as a real room's do, and
  PREDICTED in the low band follows the modes. The tail also starts sooner (Tail From reads 18 ms in
  the default room, was 26), the speakers beam their treble forward so the wall behind them answers
  darker, and later reflections are diffused. **This changes the sound of every saved Undercroft
  session**, most of all below 250 Hz.
- **Undercroft: Speakers and Ears.** In Stereo, how far apart the speakers stand (1.2 to 3.6 m) and
  how far apart the ears are (20 cm, a head, out to 160 cm, a spaced microphone pair). A wider pair
  gives a wider, less correlated wet and a weaker mono fold; at 20 cm the low end of the tail is
  nearly mono, as it is to a listener. The defaults are the old fixed spacings, so a saved session
  places its speakers and listener exactly where it did.
- **Amnesia takes a stereo image: Tap 2.** A new stepped knob beside Delay. At **Mono**, its default,
  the plugin behaves exactly as before and sessions saved under 1.2.1 recall identically. Any note
  value splits the echo: tap 1 on the left at the delay time, recirculating as ever, and a second tap
  on the right at that note value, which does not feed back. In Manual the positions read as a ratio
  against Delay.
- **Jointer: Asym.** A knob beside Knee that gives the two halves of the waveform different knees:
  +100 is a soft positive half and a hard negative one, −100 the reverse. A curve that treats the
  halves differently adds even harmonics, and the ceiling, the damage report and Stereo Link all
  still hold. 0 is the curve you had: sessions saved under 1.2.1 render identically.
- **Trammel and Keelson take an external key (sidechain).** A second input, `Sidechain`, off until
  your host routes something into it. The first moment the sidechain carries signal, the compressor
  follows it instead of its own input, and the display's header says so — a lit dot and `KEY EXT`,
  with the key's level drawn behind the gain reduction. It stays on the key until playback restarts
  or the plugin is bypassed and un-bypassed. Nothing routed, nothing changes: sessions saved under
  1.2.1 recall identically. A mono key into a stereo track is the normal case. Trammel's Input still
  sets how hard the key hits the threshold, and its SC HPF filters the key; Keelson's Threshold and
  SC HPF apply to the key.

title: Changelog > 2.0.0 > Changed
text:
- **Undercroft: the room in three dimensions.** The display is a model you can turn: drag it,
  double-click to reset. Surfaces are shaded and named by material, and each first reflection lights
  its whole path. The readings move to two lines along the foot, so the room has the screen. The
  panel is taller.
- **Keelson's panel is laid out like the hardware.** The meter runs across the top, with a needle of
  the same gain reduction beside the trace. Ratio, Attack and Release are stepped knobs, as the

title: Site > About
text:
Fruitless Research is one person: TW Walsh. I've spent decades building software and making records in parallel, and I've finally been able to bring these two disciplines together.
Usually, audio engineers describe what they hear and developers approximate it. My process removes that handoff and its translation losses. Decades of audio engineering inform my idea of what a plugin ought to sound like; measurement shows what it is actually doing, and keeps that judgement honest. Every voicing here was chosen by ear, and checked against the numbers.
The software half is the day job: I am Director of Engineering at an enterprise EdTech company. Shipping software that other people depend on has taught me to leverage data, to challenge assumptions, and to document research and decisions.

title: Site > About > The other vocation
text:
Mastering and mixing, mostly: well over a thousand records, including work for Sufjan Stevens, Nathaniel Rateliff & the Night Sweats, The Shins, Benjamin Gibbard (Death Cab for Cutie), Cold War Kids, Damien Jurado, Kristin Hersh, Clap Your Hands Say Yeah, Pernice Brothers, Starflyer 59, J. Tillman (Father John Misty), and Pedro the Lion / David Bazan. Among them a platinum-certified single, a gold-certified record, and projects that have gone on to Grammy and Oscar nominations. Production as well, including records for Starflyer 59.
Before and alongside that, on the other side of the glass: I was an official member of Pedro the Lion (Achilles Heel), Lo Tom on Barsuk with David Bazan and Jason Martin (I also produced the band's second album), Headphones, and The Soft Drugs, along with six solo albums of my own, most recently Wilderness in 2024.
These credits are not the qualification. What bears on the plugins is decades spent answerable for how a record sounds when it leaves the studio. These processors claim that every number on every panel was measured from real audio; you are entitled to know who is making that claim.

title: Site > About > Why the plugins look like this
text:
Each plugin reports modifications to your signal in metrics you can verify: the distortion a clipper added, the loudness it cost you, the decay time a plate is actually producing, the trim Auto Gain applied. Every readout is measured from the audio.
When it comes to licensing and pricing: no subscriptions, no accounts, no server for the plugin to reach, no telemetry, no activation limit, no sales or discounts. I don't want to make the product easier to sell but worse to own. A tool should still work in ten years, on a machine that has never been online.
Fruitless Research branding and design is handled by Ezra Walsh.

Reverb · Free · macOS & Windows · 14-day demo

A spring reverb, built from the physics of the coil. Free.

A spring reverb is a coil of wire with a magnet at each end: one twists it in time with the signal, the other reads what comes back. Clew solves that directly, for the long two-spring tank found in most guitar amps, instead of playing back a recording of one. - DRIVE — the vintage rack units’ input stage, from a little grit to a full snarl
- MONO for one honest tank; STEREO for two, slightly detuned
- A live view of the wet tail, drawn from your own material

text:
Reverb · $59 · macOS & Windows · 14-day demo

A room reverb whose only controls are the room.
Buy Undercroft — $59Download the 14-day demo
$59 before tax — your local sales tax, VAT or GST is added at checkout. Why? All 8 paid plugins for $359 — save $133. See the bundle, or complete it for the difference if you already own some.
Set the length, width and height, pick a material for each surface from a table of published absorption measurements, put the speakers and the listener some metres apart, and it works out what that room does to a sound: the early reflections by tracing the images of the source in every wall, the late field from the same geometry and the same table. Leave the ceiling off for a courtyard. The panel then measures its own decay time and prints it beside the one the room predicts, so you can see when a real room disagrees with the textbook.

- Dimensions, six surfaces, a sourced material table — no reverb knobs
- Mono or true Stereo: two speakers, two ears, every reflection at its own time
- Predicted and measured T60 side by side; live CPU cost
